currencies.headline: Sterling holds close to a one-year high as BoE dissent keeps hike bets alive.
currencies.commentary:
Sterling has traded firmly through the Asian and early European sessions, extending its recent advance against both the euro and the dollar. Support continues to flow from last week's Bank of England decision, where policymakers held rates for a fifth consecutive meeting but three of nine committee members voted for an immediate increase, a notably hawkish split that has kept alive market chatter about a possible hike later this year. Political uncertainty domestically has also eased somewhat following an orderly resolution to the recent Labour leadership question, removing one source of headline risk that had periodically weighed on the currency.

The mechanism at work is fairly direct: the same Middle East driven energy price pressure that has pushed independent forecasters to lift their year end UK inflation projections toward the mid-3% area is also the reason three MPC members wanted to tighten policy immediately rather than wait. That combination, a hawkish minority on the committee and a stickier inflation outlook, has been enough to see markets price a growing, if still uncertain, chance of a Bank Rate increase before year end, a sharp reversal from the cutting cycle many had expected at the start of 2026. Against a euro whose own hawkish story has faded and a dollar contending with its own rate uncertainty, sterling's relative resilience looks more structural than fleeting for now.
currencies.watchToday: No UK data is due today; the calendar stays quiet until tomorrow's BRC retail sales monitor for July. Thursday's preliminary second quarter GDP reading, alongside trade and production figures, is the week's key release for the pound.

currencies.headline: Euro drifts as its hawkish story fades against a firmer pound.
currencies.commentary:
The euro has traded on a softer footing this morning, unable to build on last week's moves and continuing to cede ground to sterling in particular. Friday's weak German industrial production figures, a sizeable miss against expectations, added to a soft patch of eurozone data that has left the currency without much independent support heading into the new week. This morning's Sentix investor confidence survey passed with limited market reaction, leaving the euro largely trading as a function of the broader dollar mood rather than its own story.

The bigger shift has been in the policy narrative. Eurozone inflation eased to 2.8% in June, down from levels that had briefly supported talk of further ECB tightening, and that cooling has effectively taken additional rate increases off the table for now, even as the central bank stays watchful of the energy price pressures flowing from the Middle East conflict. With the ECB's next full quarterly projections not due until September, the currency looks likely to keep taking its cues from relative growth and rate expectations elsewhere, a dynamic that has left it looking the weaker link among the major currencies over the past couple of weeks.
currencies.watchToday: Beyond this morning's low-impact Sentix investor confidence survey, the eurozone calendar is quiet until Wednesday's final July inflation reading from Germany. The bigger driver for the pair this week is likely to be Wednesday's US CPI report, given its implications for the dollar side of the equation.

currencies.headline: Dollar holds broadly firm as haven demand offsets a shaky jobs picture.
currencies.commentary:
The dollar has traded with a steady tone into the new week, holding much of the ground gained over recent sessions even after Friday's Nonfarm Payrolls report showed the first outright monthly decline in employment in months. That weak headline figure was muddied by an unemployment rate that actually improved and a wage growth reading that cooled sharply, leaving markets genuinely split on what it means for the Federal Reserve's next move. Rather than selling off on the soft jobs number, as textbook logic might suggest, the dollar has instead continued to draw support from its safe haven role amid ongoing geopolitical uncertainty tied to the Middle East.

That dynamic captures the unusual position the Fed finds itself in. Policymakers held rates steady for a fifth consecutive meeting in late July, but three committee members dissented in favour of an immediate increase, and a number of forecasters have shifted from expecting cuts this year to pricing a real chance of a hike, as energy driven inflation pressure builds even as the labour market cools. As a net energy exporter, the US economy is comparatively insulated from the price shock hitting import dependent economies elsewhere, reinforcing the dollar's relative appeal. That combination of hawkish rate repricing and haven flows has kept the currency well supported, though a genuine easing in Middle East tensions could quickly reverse the haven bid.
currencies.watchToday: No US data of note is due today; attention builds toward Wednesday's Consumer Price Index, the week's key release, with Thursday's Producer Price Index and jobless claims following. Tuesday's NFIB small business survey is a minor appetiser ahead of that.

currencies.headline: Yen stays on the back foot as last week's intervention gains keep fading.
currencies.commentary:
The yen has remained under pressure this morning, continuing to give back the ground it won from the rare, coordinated intervention conducted by Tokyo and Washington at the end of July. That operation, reported to have involved several trillion yen in purchases, delivered only a temporary reprieve, and the currency has since drifted back toward its earlier lows, with the retreat raising fresh doubts about how much further authorities can achieve without a genuine shift in the underlying interest rate story. This morning's Economy Watchers Survey for July is a useful, if secondary, gauge of how domestic sentiment is holding up against that backdrop.

The core issue remains the wide gap between Japanese and US interest rates. The Bank of Japan held its policy rate at 1% in an eight to one decision last week, even as it warned that core inflation could run above its 2% target, fuelling speculation about a possible hike as soon as September. Until that materialises, the yen remains one of the more vulnerable major currencies to swings in global risk appetite, having recently touched multi-decade lows against several peers, including the Australian dollar, which is itself benefiting from favourable rate expectations. Any fresh verbal or actual intervention from Tokyo would be a genuine risk event given how quickly the previous episode's gains evaporated.
currencies.watchToday: This morning's Economy Watchers Survey is a moderate release and unlikely to move the yen much on its own. The bigger swing factor this week is the widening rate gap with the US, so Wednesday's CPI report and any hints of a September Bank of Japan move are the key things to watch.

currencies.headline: Franc holds its safe-haven bid as SNB flags readiness to step in against further strength.
currencies.commentary:
The Swiss franc has traded quietly but with an underlying firm tone this morning, continuing to benefit from its traditional role as a haven of choice during periods of geopolitical stress. There is nothing on the domestic calendar today to move the currency independently, so it has largely tracked broader risk sentiment, holding steady rather than making fresh headway. That stability sits against a backdrop of exceptionally low domestic inflation, which eased further to 0.4% year on year in July, comfortably within the SNB's target range and leaving policymakers little obvious reason to shift from their current zero rate stance.

The more interesting development has been the SNB's own commentary, with officials signalling greater readiness to intervene in currency markets should the franc's safe haven appeal push it uncomfortably strong, a concern rooted in the squeeze that puts on Swiss exporters already contending with soft external demand. That is a delicate balancing act: the same global uncertainty driving demand for the franc is also the reason authorities are wary of it appreciating too far. With the policy rate anchored at zero and most economists not expecting a first move until 2027 at the earliest, the franc's path in the near term looks set to be governed more by global risk flows than by anything happening domestically.
currencies.watchToday: No Swiss data is scheduled today or for the rest of this week. The franc is likely to keep trading on broader safe-haven flows and geopolitical headlines, with the SNB's next policy assessment still some weeks away.

currencies.headline: Loonie softer as oil slips back on hopes for an Iran deal.
currencies.commentary:
The Canadian dollar has eased modestly this morning, tracking a pullback in crude oil prices after reports of progress toward a diplomatic resolution to the Iran conflict eased some of the supply fears that had driven crude sharply higher earlier in the year. As one of the more commodity-sensitive major currencies, the loonie tends to move in the same direction as oil, and the recent retreat in prices, away from the elevated levels touched at the height of the crisis, has taken some wind out of its sails even as the domestic growth story stays reasonably solid.

That domestic backdrop is actually a source of some support. Friday's Labour Force Survey showed Canada added a much stronger than expected number of jobs in July, and the unemployment rate fell to its lowest level in two years, reducing the near-term pressure on the Bank of Canada to resume cutting rates at its next meeting later this month. That combination, a resilient labour market against a softening oil price, leaves the loonie pulled in two directions: encouraged by the data, but still ultimately hostage to how the Middle East situation and its knock-on effect on energy prices develops from here.
currencies.watchToday: No Canadian data is due today. Building permits for June follow on Wednesday, a lower-tier release, with the Bank of Canada's next rate decision later this month the bigger event on the horizon and oil price direction the more immediate driver.

currencies.headline: Kiwi soft against a firm dollar even as RBNZ tightening bets stay intact.
currencies.commentary:
The New Zealand dollar has traded on a softer footing this morning, continuing to feel the pull of broad dollar strength tied to safe haven demand and shifting Fed rate expectations. That pressure has outweighed what would otherwise be a supportive domestic story: the Reserve Bank of New Zealand lifted its Official Cash Rate for the first time in more than three years in July, and markets continue to price a further quarter point increase at the September meeting after inflation accelerated well above both expectations and the Bank's own forecast in the second quarter.

The complication for the RBNZ, and for the kiwi's medium-term path, is a labour market that is deteriorating even as prices run hot. Unemployment climbed to its highest level in more than a decade in the second quarter, while wage growth has stayed subdued, a combination that leaves policymakers weighing persistent inflation against a genuinely softening jobs picture. For now, that tension has left the currency's gains more measured than the hawkish rate story alone might suggest, with near-term direction likely to keep hinging more on global dollar sentiment than on the local data flow.
currencies.watchToday: No New Zealand data is due today. The next notable release is Thursday's RBNZ Survey of Expectations for the third quarter, watched for whether the recent upward drift in inflation expectations has continued, with the Bank's September meeting the bigger event still to come.

currencies.headline: Aussie firm near multi-decade highs against the yen ahead of tomorrow's RBA decision.
currencies.commentary:
The Australian dollar has held a firm tone this morning, extending its recent advance against the yen in particular as fading Japanese intervention effects and a comparatively hawkish Reserve Bank of Australia stance work in its favour. There is nothing domestic on today's calendar, so the currency has largely traded on that cross-currency dynamic and on broader risk appetite, with China's mixed factory data from earlier in the week, an official manufacturing gauge back in contraction, doing little to dent sentiment so far.

All the attention now shifts to tomorrow's Reserve Bank decision, where a Reuters poll found every economist surveyed and all four major domestic banks expect the Board to hold its cash rate steady, though a number continue to flag the risk of one further increase later in the year given still elevated inflation. That near-unanimous expectation for a hold means the tone of the accompanying Statement on Monetary Policy and Governor Michele Bullock's press conference are likely to matter more for the Aussie's reaction than the headline decision itself. As one of the more liquid, risk-sensitive major currencies, it also remains exposed to any fresh signals out of China, still its largest trading partner, on the health of demand there.
currencies.watchToday: NAB business confidence, the RBA's rate decision and Governor Bullock's press conference are all due tomorrow, the week's key event for the Australian dollar, with a hold now the near-universal expectation. Today's session should stay comparatively quiet by contrast.

currencies.headline: Yuan steady in a tightly managed range as the PBoC keeps a firm grip on the fixing.
currencies.commentary:
The offshore yuan has traded in a narrow, well-contained range again this morning, consistent with its recent pattern of stability even as broader currency markets have seen more pronounced swings elsewhere. The People's Bank of China has continued to manage its daily reference rate closely, and record demand at last week's long-dated offshore bond auction in Hong Kong, priced at historically low yields, underscored the continued pull of Chinese assets for global investors even amid a mixed domestic growth picture.

The bigger story remains structural rather than day to day. Beijing continues to push measures aimed at cementing Hong Kong's position as the main hub for offshore yuan activity, part of a longer-running effort to internationalise the currency that sits apart from near-term data surprises. Policymakers have also made clear they are wary of the currency appreciating too quickly, favouring a gradual, closely managed path even as some analysts see room for further strength over the coming year. With Friday's trade balance data now behind it, the market's next real test for the yuan is further out, leaving the currency likely to keep taking its cues from the PBoC's daily fixing and the broader dollar trend in the meantime.
currencies.watchToday: No Chinese data of note is scheduled today. The yuan is likely to continue trading on the PBoC's daily fixing decisions and broader dollar direction, with the next major domestic release still some weeks away.

currencies.headline: Rand firm as falling oil offsets a historically tricky seasonal month.
currencies.commentary:
The South African rand has continued to firm this morning, building on its recovery from last month's multi-month low. A retreat in crude oil prices, easing on hopes for a diplomatic resolution to the Iran conflict, has been particularly supportive given South Africa's status as a net energy importer, while a broadly softer US dollar has added a further tailwind. Trading has been orderly rather than sharply directional, with the currency continuing to claw back ground lost during the worst of the geopolitical scare earlier in the year.

That improvement comes despite the South African Reserve Bank holding its policy rate steady at 7% in a split vote late last month, with inflation still running above the top of its target range, a combination that leaves the rand's recent strength looking more a function of favourable external conditions than a genuine improvement in the domestic story. August also carries a reputation as a seasonally difficult month for the currency, a pattern worth bearing in mind even during a spell of relative calm. Tomorrow's Quarterly Labour Force Survey is the next real test of whether the domestic backdrop can offer the currency support of its own, rather than leaving it dependent on oil and broader risk sentiment.
currencies.watchToday: No South African data is due today, but tomorrow brings the high-importance Quarterly Labour Force Survey for the second quarter, watched closely given the persistently high unemployment rate. Beyond that, oil prices and broader dollar direction remain the more immediate drivers.

currencies.headline: Sterling eases back from its best levels as the dollar firms on renewed Hormuz jitters.
currencies.commentary:
Since this morning's update, sterling has lost a little of its shine, slipping back from the multi-week high touched against the dollar late last week as a broader bout of dollar strength took hold through the European afternoon. The move has had little to do with anything domestic, the UK calendar remains empty today, and everything to do with a firmer dollar, as renewed uncertainty over whether the Strait of Hormuz will actually reopen sent traders back toward havens. Sterling has held up better against the euro, where it continues to benefit from the more hawkish Bank of England backdrop.

The pullback looks more like profit taking after a strong run than a genuine change in the pound's underlying story. Last week's hawkish split on the Bank of England's committee, with three members voting for an immediate hike, remains intact, and political uncertainty has continued to ease following the resolution of the Labour leadership question. With the domestic calendar bare until tomorrow, sterling is likely to keep taking its cue from the dollar's mood into the New York open.
currencies.watchToday: Nothing further is scheduled on the UK calendar for the rest of today. Attention turns to tomorrow's BRC retail sales monitor for July, an early read on consumer demand, with Thursday's preliminary second quarter GDP reading the week's more significant release.

currencies.headline: Euro stays rangebound, still lacking a story of its own as the dollar firms.
currencies.commentary:
The euro has had a quiet afternoon, with this morning's Sentix investor confidence survey passing without much reaction and no fresh domestic headlines to give the currency independent direction. Instead, it has mostly drifted alongside the broader dollar's afternoon rebound, driven by renewed nervousness over Middle East shipping routes rather than anything from Frankfurt, leaving the single currency on a softer footing against the dollar while holding up only marginally better against the pound.

The bigger picture for the euro remains unchanged since this morning: last week's soft German industrial production figures continue to weigh on sentiment, and there is little on the immediate horizon to change that. Markets are increasingly treating the euro as a residual, a currency whose near-term direction is set more by what the dollar and the pound are doing than by anything happening within the eurozone itself. That is likely to remain the case until fresh data arrives later in the week.
currencies.watchToday: The eurozone calendar has nothing left today. Wednesday brings the final German inflation reading for July, though the bigger driver for the pair this week is likely to be Wednesday's US Consumer Price Index and what it means for the dollar side of the equation.

currencies.headline: Dollar firms into the afternoon as renewed Hormuz uncertainty revives haven demand.
currencies.commentary:
The dollar has picked up a firmer tone through the European afternoon, reversing some of Friday's softness after reports that Iran will demand concessions from Washington before actually reopening the Strait of Hormuz reignited the same safe haven bid that has repeatedly supported the currency through this year's Middle East tensions. That has come even as US equity futures traded cautiously, with Dow futures dipping as oil climbed while the S&P 500 and Nasdaq held closer to record territory, a split that reflects the market's difficulty pricing the net effect of higher energy costs against still resilient risk appetite.

The renewed haven bid has, for now, pushed Friday's weak Nonfarm Payrolls report further into the background, even though the debate over what a genuine decline in employment means for the Federal Reserve has not gone away. With no US data due today, the dollar's next real test comes Wednesday, when the Consumer Price Index will help settle whether investors should be leaning toward a softer Fed or a more cautious one.
currencies.watchToday: No US data is left on today's calendar. Tomorrow's NFIB small business survey is a minor appetiser ahead of Wednesday's Consumer Price Index, the week's key release, with Producer Price Index and jobless claims data following on Thursday.

currencies.headline: Yen drifts a touch softer as the dollar's haven bid outmuscles its own.
currencies.commentary:
The yen has continued to give ground through the afternoon, extending the gradual fade of the gains won from late July's coordinated intervention. This morning's Economy Watchers Survey passed with little fanfare, landing close to expectations and offering no fresh catalyst either way. Instead, the yen's afternoon weakness has come almost entirely from the dollar's own resurgence, a reminder that when both currencies are in demand as havens simultaneously, as has been the case today amid the renewed Hormuz uncertainty, it is the wider interest rate gap that tends to decide which one wins out.

That dynamic continues to complicate the yen's traditional defensive role. With US yields still comfortably above Japanese ones, the currency has struggled to attract the kind of haven flows it might once have commanded automatically during bouts of geopolitical stress, leaving traders instead focused on the prospect of further intervention or a genuine shift in Bank of Japan policy as the more reliable triggers for a sustained turnaround.
currencies.watchToday: Nothing further is scheduled on the Japanese calendar today. The wider dollar yen interest rate gap remains the key swing factor this week, with Wednesday's US CPI report and any hints of a September Bank of Japan move the things to watch.

currencies.headline: Franc holds its safe haven bid steady as Hormuz jitters keep risk appetite in check.
currencies.commentary:
The Swiss franc has had a quiet but firm afternoon, continuing to benefit from its role as a haven of choice as renewed uncertainty over the Strait of Hormuz kept a lid on broader risk appetite. With no domestic data to react to, the currency has essentially tracked the same geopolitical headlines driving the dollar's afternoon strength, holding its ground rather than making fresh headway of its own.

The franc's underlying story has not changed since this morning: exceptionally low domestic inflation, which eased further in July, leaves the Swiss National Bank with little obvious reason to alter its stance, and the currency remains free to trade largely as a function of global risk sentiment. That leaves it well positioned to extend its firmness if today's Middle East uncertainty deepens, though a genuine easing in tensions could just as quickly take some of the shine off.
currencies.watchToday: No Swiss data is scheduled for the rest of today or this week. The franc is likely to keep trading on broader safe haven flows and Middle East headlines, with the Swiss National Bank's next policy assessment still some weeks away.

currencies.headline: Loonie claws back this morning's losses as oil turns higher on renewed Hormuz doubts.
currencies.commentary:
The Canadian dollar has reversed course since this morning, firming alongside a rebound in crude oil after reports that Iran will seek concessions from Washington before allowing the Strait of Hormuz to reopen fully undercut the optimism that had briefly pulled oil lower last week. Crude has climbed back above the levels seen a few sessions ago, extending a run of gains, and with the loonie's fortunes so closely tied to oil, that shift has been enough to put a firmer floor under the currency through the European afternoon.

The episode is a useful reminder of just how sensitive the Canadian dollar remains to headline risk out of the Middle East, arguably more than any other major currency covered here. A durable resolution to the Hormuz standoff would likely see oil give back today's gains and take the loonie with it, while any further hardening in Iran's position could extend the rally further. With no Canadian data due today, that headline sensitivity is likely to persist into tomorrow.
currencies.watchToday: No Canadian data is left on today's calendar. Wednesday's building permits release for June is a lower tier data point, with oil price direction and any further developments in the Iran-Oman shipping talks the more immediate driver into tomorrow.

currencies.headline: Kiwi slips back from recent highs as broad dollar strength returns.
currencies.commentary:
The New Zealand dollar has given back some of its recent outperformance this afternoon, as the same renewed haven demand for the dollar that has weighed on other higher yielding currencies took hold following fresh doubts over the Strait of Hormuz's reopening. That marks a shift from this morning's tone, when the kiwi was holding close to a two month high on the back of last month's Reserve Bank of New Zealand rate hike and hawkish inflation expectations.

The underlying policy story has not changed. Markets continue to price in a further quarter point RBNZ hike next month after second quarter inflation ran hotter than expected, and that remains the primary reason the kiwi has outperformed most peers over recent weeks. Today's pullback looks like it owes more to the broader dollar's afternoon strength than to any reassessment of New Zealand's own rate path, which should leave the currency well placed to resume its advance once the current bout of dollar demand fades.
currencies.watchToday: Nothing further is scheduled on the New Zealand calendar today. Thursday's RBNZ Survey of Expectations for the third quarter is the next notable release, watched for whether inflation expectations have continued to drift higher, with the Bank's September meeting the bigger event still to come.

currencies.headline: Aussie stays subdued, caught between dollar strength and tomorrow's RBA decision.
currencies.commentary:
The Australian dollar has traded quietly but on a softer footing this afternoon, unable to escape the pull of broader dollar strength that has weighed on most higher yielding currencies as renewed Hormuz uncertainty revived haven demand. With no domestic data to offer a counterweight and China's own growth signals still mixed, the Aussie has largely taken its cue from the same cross market forces driving the dollar rather than anything specific to Australia.

Most of the market's attention, though, is really fixed on tomorrow, when the Reserve Bank of Australia delivers its rate decision alongside its quarterly Statement on Monetary Policy and Governor Bullock's press conference. A hold at current levels is now close to the consensus view after June's softer than expected inflation reading, but the accompanying language and forecasts will matter more than the decision itself for where the currency goes next. That makes today's quiet trade look very much like the calm before a potentially busier session tomorrow.
currencies.watchToday: Tomorrow brings the week's key event for the Australian dollar: NAB business confidence, the RBA's rate decision and Statement on Monetary Policy, and Governor Bullock's press conference, all in quick succession. A hold is the near universal expectation, so the tone of the accompanying commentary is likely to matter more than the decision itself.

currencies.headline: Yuan stays tightly managed as the PBoC sets a notably firmer fixing than expected.
currencies.commentary:
The offshore yuan has continued to trade in its now familiar narrow range this afternoon, with the People's Bank of China setting today's daily reference rate meaningfully stronger than analysts had pencilled in, a signal that policymakers remain uncomfortable with the pace of recent depreciation pressure even as they continue to tolerate gradual weakness over time. That firmer fixing has helped keep the currency stable through the session, consistent with its recent pattern of resisting the sharper swings seen elsewhere in currency markets.

The bigger picture remains structural rather than day to day. Beijing continues to balance support for exporters, who benefit from a weaker currency, against the risk of unsettling capital flows if depreciation runs too far too fast, and today's firmer fixing looks like a small nudge in the latter direction. With no Chinese data due today, the yuan is likely to keep trading on the PBoC's daily fixing decisions and the broader dollar's afternoon direction rather than any domestic catalyst of its own.
currencies.watchToday: No Chinese data is scheduled for the rest of today. The next notable domestic release is Thursday's money supply and lending data for July, with the PBoC's daily fixing and broader dollar moves remaining the more immediate drivers in the meantime.

currencies.headline: Rand gives back a little ground as rising oil offsets earlier dollar softness.
currencies.commentary:
The South African rand has eased slightly since this morning, as a renewed climb in oil prices took some of the shine off a currency that had been firming on the back of a broadly softer dollar. As a net energy importer, South Africa's currency tends to suffer when crude rises, and today's jump on the back of fresh doubts over the Strait of Hormuz's reopening has been enough to interrupt the rand's recent recovery, even as the broader dollar backdrop remains only modestly supportive relative to where it stood a few weeks ago.

The move looks like a pause rather than a reversal of the rand's longer term recovery from last month's multi month low. That improvement has rested on a stronger domestic growth picture, healthy public finances and confidence in the South African Reserve Bank's commitment to its inflation target, none of which has changed today. Attention is already turning to tomorrow's Quarterly Labour Force Survey, a closely watched gauge of the persistently high unemployment rate that could set the tone for the rand into the rest of the week.
currencies.watchToday: Nothing further is scheduled on the South African calendar today. Tomorrow's Quarterly Labour Force Survey for the second quarter is a high importance release given the country's persistently high jobless rate, with oil prices and broader dollar direction remaining the more immediate drivers until then.

currencies.headline: Sterling drifts with the dollar as traders brace for today's US jobs report, UK calendar quiet.
currencies.commentary:
Sterling has taken its cue from broader dollar dynamics rather than anything domestic this morning, drifting a touch softer after the Bank of England joined the Federal Reserve in holding policy steady earlier this week. With no fresh UK data to chew on, the pound has largely tracked the dollar's own mood, easing modestly as renewed haven demand for the greenback crept back in on the back of shifting rhetoric around US-Iran diplomacy. Trading has been fairly contained rather than directional, consistent with a market that is essentially marking time until this afternoon's Nonfarm Payrolls release.

The bigger picture for sterling remains a tug of war between persistent UK political and fiscal uncertainty, which continues to weigh on sentiment, and a domestic inflation picture that has kept the BoE cautious about how quickly it can resume cutting rates. That leaves the pound more exposed than some peers to swings in risk appetite and to the dollar's own trajectory, since there is little homegrown data this week to give it independent direction. For now, sterling is essentially a passenger, its near-term path likely to be set more by what happens in Washington and at the Fed than in London.
currencies.watchToday: No UK data is due today; sterling's near-term direction is more likely to be set by this afternoon's US jobs report and the broader dollar mood. Attention turns to Tuesday's BRC retail sales monitor for a first read on UK consumer spending in July.

currencies.headline: Euro edges softer against a firmer dollar as German trade data and payrolls both loom.
currencies.commentary:
The euro has eased modestly this morning as the dollar found a bit of composure heading into today's US jobs report, extending a gentle pullback from earlier in the week. Attention within the eurozone itself is on this morning's German industrial production and trade balance figures for June, a timely check on whether the recent improvement in German factory orders, which jumped more than expected in May, is translating into an actual pickup in output. Trading has been orderly rather than dramatic, with the single currency still holding within recent ranges against both the dollar and sterling.

The broader backdrop remains one of a eurozone economy leaning on Germany's large fiscal stimulus programme to work its way through the system, even as the ECB has nudged up its own inflation projections for 2026 and 2027, a mildly hawkish signal that argues against near-term rate cuts. That leaves the euro's fate this morning tied less to its own story and more to the dollar's, with today's Nonfarm Payrolls likely to matter more for the pair's direction than anything on the domestic calendar. A convincing German data beat could offer some independent support, but the path of least resistance has been to trade as the dollar's mirror image.
currencies.watchToday: German industrial production and trade balance for June are due at 07:00 UK time, a read on whether the recent pickup in factory orders is feeding through to actual output. Beyond that, this afternoon's US payrolls report is likely to be the bigger driver, with Sentix investor confidence the next notable eurozone release on Monday.

currencies.headline: Dollar holds steady into a pivotal Nonfarm Payrolls print after a string of soft labour data.
currencies.commentary:
The dollar has traded with a slightly firmer tone into this afternoon's headline event, clawing back some composure after a choppy week, though the real test comes at 13:30 UK time when July's Nonfarm Payrolls lands. June's report was a significant disappointment at just 57,000 jobs, and this week's ADP private payrolls figure for July undershot even more sharply at 44,000 against expectations nearer 70,000, adding to nerves that the labour market is cooling faster than the Fed would like. Estimates for today's official figure are unusually wide, ranging from roughly 40,000 to 120,000 across major banks, underlining just how uncertain the outcome is.

The stakes are high because the report sits squarely at the centre of the debate over whether the Fed cuts rates in September. A weak print, particularly paired with a rise in the 4.2% unemployment rate, would harden expectations for a cut and likely pressure the dollar; a strong beat would support the more hawkish members who dissented at July's meeting and could see the dollar extend its recent firmness. Fed Governor Lisa Cook's comments yesterday were parsed closely for hints on where she sits, and Richmond Fed President Thomas Barkin speaks again this afternoon, just hours after the data, for the market's first policymaker reaction.
currencies.watchToday: July's Nonfarm Payrolls, average hourly earnings and unemployment rate land at 13:30 UK time, the single biggest release of the week for every major currency pair. Richmond Fed President Barkin speaks shortly after at 15:00, with consumer credit data rounding out the day.

currencies.headline: Yen slips back as intervention gains fade, keeping authorities on alert.
currencies.commentary:
The yen has given back a significant share of the gains it won from last Friday's rare, coordinated Japan-US intervention, the first joint currency operation between the two countries since 2011, as broader dollar firmness has crept back in ahead of today's payrolls report. Japan's Ministry of Finance is estimated to have spent tens of billions of dollars buying yen during that intervention, and officials from both countries have signalled they stand ready to act again if the slide resumes, keeping traders on alert for any fresh verbal or actual intervention today. Domestic data this morning, a preliminary leading economic index and machine tool orders, are both low-impact and unlikely to move the currency much on their own.

The underlying driver has not changed: a wide gap between a Bank of Japan still moving only gradually on rate hikes and a Federal Reserve seen as edging toward cuts, a differential that has pushed 30-year Japanese government bond yields to their highest in three decades and fuelled the currency's earlier slide to multi-decade lows. A softer US payrolls report today would ease some of that pressure by weighing on Treasury yields and the dollar broadly, offering the yen genuine relief rather than the temporary reprieve intervention alone can provide; a strong print would test officials' resolve to defend the currency all over again.
currencies.watchToday: Japan's leading economic index and machine tool orders for July, both preliminary and low-impact, are due early this morning. The bigger swing factor is this afternoon's US jobs report, given its direct bearing on the yield gap that has driven the yen's recent weakness, with the Economy Watchers Survey the next domestic release on Monday.

currencies.headline: Franc steady as SNB's zero-rate stance stays entrenched on soft inflation.
currencies.commentary:
The Swiss franc has traded quietly this morning, holding broadly steady as markets await this afternoon's US payrolls report for fresh direction. There is little domestically to move the currency today beyond the SECO consumer climate survey for the third quarter, a low-impact release. The franc's recent behaviour has been consistent with its position as one of the year's more structurally resilient currencies, underpinned by its haven appeal at times of geopolitical stress even as its own yield remains anchored at zero.

Swiss inflation eased to 0.4% year on year in July from 0.5% in June, its softest reading in four months and comfortably within the SNB's 0 to 2% target range, reinforcing the central bank's case for staying on hold. Unemployment has drifted higher through the year as exporters feel the pinch from a strong franc and soft external demand, a reminder that the SNB's caution cuts both ways: too-low inflation and a strong currency squeezing trade are exactly the conditions that could eventually force a rethink. For now though, with most economists not pencilling in a first hike until 2028, the franc's low-yield, high-safety profile looks set to persist.
currencies.watchToday: Switzerland's SECO consumer climate survey for the third quarter is due this morning, a low-impact release. With little else on the Swiss calendar this week, the franc is likely to keep taking its cues from broader risk sentiment and safe-haven flows tied to global events.

currencies.headline: Loonie firms with oil ahead of a double dose of Canadian and US jobs data.
currencies.commentary:
The Canadian dollar has firmed modestly this morning, helped by a rebound in crude oil prices, its key commodity anchor, as it heads into a genuinely high-stakes session. Canada's own Labour Force Survey for July lands at the same moment as the US Nonfarm Payrolls report this afternoon, giving traders a rare simultaneous read on both economies' labour markets. That timing matters: a weak showing on either side of the border could move the loonie sharply, while a divergence between the two, a soft US print alongside a firm Canadian one or vice versa, would be a genuinely fresh signal for the pair rather than just noise.

Context matters here too. Canada's unemployment rate stood at 6.5% in June, and the Bank of Canada has been content to stay on hold until its next decision on 27 August, meaning today's data feeds directly into how much slack policymakers think is building before that meeting. Oil's role as the loonie's other major swing factor is not to be discounted either: with crude having recovered some ground this week, further strength there could cushion the currency even if the jobs data disappoints, while a renewed slide in prices would compound any labour market weakness.
currencies.watchToday: Canada's Labour Force Survey for July, a high-importance release, lands at 13:30 UK time alongside the US jobs report, with the Ivey PMI following at 15:00. The Bank of Canada's next rate decision is not until 27 August, so today's data will shape expectations heading into that meeting.

currencies.headline: Kiwi holds gains from July's rate hike even as the labour market shows real cracks.
currencies.commentary:
The New Zealand dollar has held up relatively well in recent sessions, still benefiting from last month's Reserve Bank of New Zealand decision to lift the Official Cash Rate 25 basis points to 2.50%, its first hike in more than three years. That move followed inflation accelerating to 4.1% year on year in the second quarter, well above both expectations and the RBNZ's own forecast, and markets have continued to price a real chance of further tightening in September. Yesterday's RBNZ inflation expectations survey for the third quarter, a lower-impact release, is being read for early signs of whether that hawkish repricing is starting to feed through to businesses' own forecasts.

The complication is the labour market, where New Zealand's unemployment rate climbed to 5.6% in the second quarter, its highest since 2015, even as annual wage growth stayed subdued at 2.0%. That combination, hot inflation alongside a softening jobs market, puts the RBNZ in a genuinely difficult spot and is a big part of why the kiwi's gains have been more measured than the rate move alone might suggest. With no domestic data due for the rest of this week, the currency is likely to keep trading more on global risk sentiment and the broader RBNZ policy narrative than on fresh local news.
currencies.watchToday: No New Zealand data is scheduled for the rest of this week following yesterday's inflation expectations survey. The kiwi is likely to keep taking its direction from broader risk sentiment and the market's evolving read on the RBNZ's September meeting.

currencies.headline: Aussie steady as soft inflation all but rules out an RBA hike next week.
currencies.commentary:
The Australian dollar has held a firm tone this morning, supported by a generally upbeat global risk mood and by a mixed but not alarming set of signals out of China, its largest trading partner. China's official manufacturing PMI slipped back into contraction at 49.2 for July, but the private RatingDog survey offered a somewhat less downbeat cross-check, easing only to 50.9 from 51.7 and still signalling modest expansion, even though it undershot the 51.5 forecast. There is no Australian data due today, so the currency has largely been trading on these broader external cues rather than anything homegrown.

The bigger domestic story is next Tuesday's Reserve Bank of Australia decision, where softer than expected second-quarter inflation data has virtually ruled out a rate increase, a notable shift after Governor Michele Bullock had earlier left the door open to further hikes. That repricing has capped some of the Aussie's upside even as risk sentiment has been supportive, leaving the currency in a holding pattern ahead of the meeting. As one of the more liquid, risk-sensitive major currencies, the Aussie remains especially exposed to any swings in global sentiment or fresh China data between now and then.
currencies.watchToday: No Australian data is due today. NAB business confidence and the RBA's interest rate decision, alongside Governor Bullock's press conference, are the key events to watch on Tuesday, with a hold now the widely expected outcome.

currencies.headline: Yuan steady near recent strong levels as PBoC keeps its fixing on the firm side.
currencies.commentary:
The offshore yuan has traded in a tight, well-contained range this morning, continuing its recent run as one of the steadier major currencies. The People's Bank of China has kept setting its daily reference rate on the firm side of expectations, a signal of continued official comfort with the currency's recent resilience even as the broader growth picture stays mixed. Today's focus is July's trade balance, due at 04:00 UK time, a release watched closely both for what it says about Chinese export demand and for what it implies for commodity-linked currencies like the Australian and New Zealand dollars, given China's role as their largest trading partner.

The bigger story remains structural rather than day to day. Beijing has kept pushing measures to deepen Hong Kong's role as the main offshore yuan hub, part of a longer-running push to internationalise the currency that sits apart from the near-term data flow. That, combined with the PBoC's steady hand on the fix, has been enough to keep the yuan anchored even against a genuinely mixed factory backdrop, with the official manufacturing PMI back in contraction while the private equivalent still points to modest, if slowing, expansion.
currencies.watchToday: China's July trade balance is due at 04:00 UK time this morning, a release with particular relevance for how much support Chinese demand is providing to the Australian and New Zealand dollars. Beyond that, the yuan's path this week is likely to stay tied to the PBoC's daily fixing decisions and broader dollar direction.

currencies.headline: Rand holds near its best levels in weeks as softer oil and risk appetite offset a hawkish inflation backdrop.
currencies.commentary:
The South African rand has firmed to around its strongest point in several weeks, recovering further from the more than three-month low it touched in late July. Softer oil prices, with Brent slipping back under the 80 dollar mark, have provided some relief given South Africa's heavy reliance on energy imports, while a broadly improved global risk mood has also lent support to the currency alongside other emerging market peers. That recovery comes despite a genuinely hawkish domestic inflation backdrop that would normally argue for more caution around the currency.

The South African Reserve Bank held its repurchase rate at 7% on 23 July, in a split four to two vote, with headline inflation running at 5.0% and core inflation at 4.1%, both above the top of the 3% plus or minus 1 percentage point target band the SARB is meant to defend. That combination, elevated inflation alongside a bank reluctant to hike further, is a reminder that the rand's recent firmness owes more to favourable external conditions than to domestic strength, leaving it vulnerable if oil prices or global risk sentiment turn. August has historically been a seasonally weak month for the rand, a pattern worth bearing in mind even during a period of relative calm.
currencies.watchToday: No South African data is due today. The domestic calendar stays quiet until Tuesday's Quarterly Labour Force Survey for the second quarter, a high-importance release, with broader dollar direction and global risk sentiment the more immediate drivers until then.

currencies.headline: Sterling firms as Mideast de-escalation hopes power a broader risk rally into payrolls.
currencies.commentary:
Sterling has picked up since this morning's update, tracking a broader lift in risk appetite as reports of progress toward a deal to end the five month US-Iran standoff over the Strait of Hormuz have circulated through the European afternoon. With no domestic data to digest, the pound has essentially ridden that wave, extending its earlier gains against a dollar that has struggled to build on this week's firmness even as traders count down to the Nonfarm Payrolls release. Gilts have also caught a bid alongside the wider improvement in sentiment.

The move underlines just how thin the UK's own story has been this week: rather than domestic policy or data driving sterling, it is swings in global risk appetite, first from Fed rhetoric, then oil market gyrations, and now Middle East diplomacy, that have set the pound's course. That leaves sterling's afternoon gains looking somewhat fragile, since a soft or hot payrolls surprise could easily overwhelm the current mood in either direction within the hour.
currencies.watchToday: No UK data remains on today's calendar; sterling's next moves hinge on the market reaction to this afternoon's US payrolls report and Fed commentary. The BRC retail sales monitor on Tuesday is the next domestic release, offering the first read on UK consumer spending in July.

currencies.headline: Euro drifts in a narrow range as German output data disappoints and traders await payrolls.
currencies.commentary:
The euro has done little since this morning beyond consolidating within a tight band, with this morning's German industrial production figures landing softer than hoped: output rose only slightly in June, a sharp deceleration from May's pace, even as the automotive sector provided a bright spot. That cooler reading has been largely shrugged off by the single currency, which has instead taken its cue from the same wait and see mood gripping most major pairs ahead of this afternoon's Nonfarm Payrolls.

The muted reaction to the German data says as much about where the market's attention is as it does about the eurozone's own prospects: with the ECB having already nudged up its inflation projections and ruled out near-term cuts, and ahead of a payrolls print with genuinely wide ranging estimates, few traders want to commit to a fresh euro view before Washington's number lands. The broader improvement in risk sentiment tied to easing Middle East tensions has offered a mild tailwind, but it has been dollar dynamics, not eurozone fundamentals, doing the heavy lifting today.
currencies.watchToday: Nothing further is due on the eurozone calendar today; the focus stays squarely on this afternoon's US jobs report given its outsized bearing on the pair. Monday's Sentix investor confidence survey is the next scheduled eurozone release.

currencies.headline: Dollar holds a tight range with Nonfarm Payrolls just minutes away.
currencies.commentary:
The dollar has traded in a notably narrow band through the European afternoon, essentially parked as traders wait for July's Nonfarm Payrolls, due at 13:30 UK time, alongside average hourly earnings and the unemployment rate. Risk sentiment has firmed since this morning on reports of progress toward ending the US-Iran standoff over the Strait of Hormuz, a shift that has taken some safe haven bid out of the dollar even as it heads into the year's most consequential jobs report with a still relatively firm underlying tone.

The stakes have not diminished since this morning: June's payrolls badly missed at 57,000 and July's ADP private payrolls print undershot even more sharply, fuelling real uncertainty over whether the labour market is cooling faster than the Fed anticipated. Bank estimates for today's figure span an unusually wide range, and the outcome is likely to settle the debate over a September rate cut in one direction or the other within minutes of release, making the current calm look more like the eye of the storm than genuine resolution.
currencies.watchToday: July's Nonfarm Payrolls, average hourly earnings and the unemployment rate land at 13:30 UK time, arguably the month's single biggest release. Fed's Thomas Barkin speaks shortly after at 15:00, with US consumer credit data following at the same time.

currencies.headline: Yen steadies after giving back nearly half its intervention gains, with eyes on payrolls.
currencies.commentary:
The yen has found a bit of calm since this morning after a rough week in which it surrendered close to half the gains won from last Friday's coordinated Japan-US intervention, the first joint currency operation between the two countries since 1998. That fade has left traders speculating officials could step in again if the slide resumes, though there has been no fresh sign of intervention through the European afternoon. This morning's Japanese data, a preliminary leading index and machine tool orders, passed with little market reaction, as expected.

The core tension has not changed: a Bank of Japan still moving cautiously on rates against a Federal Reserve seen as edging toward cuts, a gap that pushed the currency to its earlier lows and prompted the rare joint intervention in the first place. This afternoon's payrolls report is the more meaningful swing factor now, since a soft print would ease pressure on the yen by weighing on Treasury yields and the dollar broadly, while a strong number would test how much appetite officials in Tokyo and Washington really have to defend the currency again.
currencies.watchToday: No further Japanese data is due today. The US payrolls report is the more immediate driver given its bearing on the yield gap behind the yen's recent weakness, with Monday's Economy Watchers Survey the next domestic release.

currencies.headline: Franc little changed as a softer than feared consumer climate reading confirms a fragile but stabilising picture.
currencies.commentary:
The Swiss franc has traded quietly through the European afternoon, holding much the same broadly steady tone flagged this morning. The SECO consumer climate survey for the third quarter, released this morning, ticked up modestly from the prior quarter's reading, still deeply negative but a touch less so, consistent with a domestic economy that is stabilising rather than genuinely improving. There has been little else to move the currency since, and it has largely tracked the same cautious, wait and watch mood as its major peers ahead of payrolls.

The franc's underlying story remains unchanged from this morning: rock bottom Swiss inflation keeps the SNB entrenched at zero rates, while the currency's haven appeal continues to draw support whenever geopolitical risk flares, as it has done on and off this week around the Strait of Hormuz. With risk sentiment having improved a touch into the afternoon on hopes of a US-Iran de-escalation, some of that haven bid has eased back, though the franc's low yield, high safety profile looks set to persist regardless of today's swings.
currencies.watchToday: No further Swiss data is due today or scheduled for the coming days. The franc is likely to keep taking its lead from broader risk sentiment, the payrolls reaction, and any fresh developments around the Middle East.

currencies.headline: Loonie steadies for a high-stakes double header as Canadian and US jobs data both land at 13:30.
currencies.commentary:
The Canadian dollar has held a fairly tight range through the European afternoon, consolidating this morning's modest firmness as traders position for the coming hour's twin releases: Canada's Labour Force Survey and the US Nonfarm Payrolls, both due at 13:30 UK time. Crude oil, the loonie's key commodity anchor, has stayed on the softer side into the afternoon after this week's sharp swings, tempering some of the earlier support the currency drew from firmer prices.

The setup is genuinely two-sided: a weak print on either side of the border could move the loonie sharply, and a divergence between the two, a soft US number alongside a firmer Canadian one or vice versa, would be a fresh signal rather than noise traders can shrug off. With the Bank of Canada on hold until its 27 August decision, today's data feeds directly into how much labour market slack policymakers are likely to see before then, leaving the loonie more exposed to the next hour than to anything that has happened so far this afternoon.
currencies.watchToday: Canada's Labour Force Survey lands at 13:30 UK time alongside the US jobs report, with the Ivey PMI following at 15:00. The Bank of Canada's next decision is not due until 27 August.

currencies.headline: Kiwi holds steady with little fresh to react to since this morning.
currencies.commentary:
The New Zealand dollar has been genuinely quiet through the European afternoon, with no domestic data or headlines to move it since this morning's update. It continues to hold up reasonably well on the back of last month's Reserve Bank of New Zealand rate hike and the hot inflation print that prompted it, though gains have stayed measured given the parallel softening in the labour market flagged this morning. The currency has largely tracked the same broader improvement in risk appetite lifting other growth sensitive currencies into the payrolls release.

With little homegrown news this week, the kiwi's path continues to be set more by global forces than by anything domestic: swings in risk sentiment, the dollar's reaction to this afternoon's jobs data, and the market's evolving view of the RBNZ's September meeting all matter more right now than any single New Zealand release. That leaves the currency in a genuinely wait and see posture, with today's calm likely to be tested more by events in Washington over the next hour than by anything happening at home.
currencies.watchToday: No New Zealand data is scheduled for the rest of today or the remainder of this week. Broader risk sentiment, the payrolls reaction, and the evolving read on the RBNZ's September meeting remain the key drivers to watch.

currencies.headline: Aussie firms modestly with risk appetite as traders count down to next week's RBA decision.
currencies.commentary:
The Australian dollar has firmed a touch since this morning, benefiting from the same improvement in global risk sentiment that has lifted other currencies this afternoon on hopes that the US and Iran are moving closer to ending their standoff over the Strait of Hormuz. There has been no fresh Australian data to react to, so the currency has essentially traded as a proxy for that broader mood, alongside the usual sensitivity to China headlines given China's status as its largest trading partner.

The bigger event remains Tuesday's Reserve Bank of Australia decision, where a hold is now the widely expected outcome after softer than forecast inflation data all but ruled out a hike this month. That backdrop continues to cap the Aussie's upside even on days like today when risk appetite is supportive, leaving the currency's afternoon firmness looking more like a reflection of the broader mood than a genuine standalone move. This afternoon's payrolls report is the next real test of whether that mood holds into the weekend.
currencies.watchToday: No Australian data is due for the rest of today. NAB business confidence and the RBA's interest rate decision, along with Governor Bullock's press conference, are the key events to watch on Tuesday, with a hold the widely expected outcome.

currencies.headline: Yuan holds firm after July trade data beats forecasts on another surge in exports.
currencies.commentary:
The offshore yuan has stayed well contained through the European afternoon after this morning's July trade balance came in stronger than expected, with the surplus easing back from June's near record level but still beating forecasts as exports grew robustly on a year on year basis. Imports also picked up more than expected, a detail worth noting since it points to somewhat firmer domestic demand alongside the export strength, rather than the surplus being driven purely by weak imports.

The currency's underlying resilience continues to owe as much to the PBoC's steady, supportive daily fixing as to the trade data itself, keeping the yuan anchored near its strongest levels in several years even as the broader growth picture stays mixed. With China's role as the largest trading partner for both Australia and New Zealand, this morning's export strength offers some cross-currency support for the Aussie and kiwi too, reinforcing the improved risk mood seen across the region this afternoon.
currencies.watchToday: No further Chinese data is scheduled for the rest of today or the coming week. The yuan's path is likely to stay tied to the PBoC's daily fixing decisions and to broader dollar direction around this afternoon's payrolls report.

currencies.headline: Rand extends its advance to fresh multi-week highs as gold's rally and calmer oil lend support.
currencies.commentary:
The South African rand has built on this morning's gains through the European afternoon, helped by gold's continued surge toward its best weekly performance since January, up more than 5% over the week, alongside a further easing in oil prices as hopes grow that the US and Iran are moving toward ending their standoff over the Strait of Hormuz. That combination, a firmer gold price and calmer energy markets, has proven a supportive backdrop for the rand even as the currency's own inflation story remains unresolved.

The improvement sits somewhat awkwardly alongside the domestic picture flagged this morning: a South African Reserve Bank that held rates in a split vote and inflation running above target on both a headline and core basis. That combination would normally argue for caution, a reminder that today's rand strength owes more to favourable external conditions, gold, oil and broader risk appetite, than to any change in the domestic outlook, leaving it vulnerable to a reversal in any of those three if sentiment turns.
currencies.watchToday: No South African data is due for the rest of today. Tuesday's Quarterly Labour Force Survey for the second quarter is the next high-importance release, with broader dollar direction and this afternoon's payrolls reaction the more immediate drivers until then.

currencies.headline: Sterling steady after last month's split BoE hold, with only minor data on the calendar today.
currencies.commentary:
Sterling has traded in a narrow range overnight, holding broadly steady as markets continue to digest the Bank of England's decision to keep Bank Rate at 3.75% on 30 July. The six to three vote split was closer than many had expected, with three committee members pushing for a hike, and that hawkish undertone has kept the pound reasonably well supported even as today's UK calendar offers little of substance beyond house price and construction readings. With no fresh domestic catalyst, sterling is largely taking its cue from the broader dollar backdrop and positioning ahead of Friday's US employment report.

The pound's resilience owes much to the policy gap it has opened up against the euro, with Bank of England rates sitting well above the European Central Bank's, one of the widest such gaps in years and a key reason sterling has held close to multi-year highs against the single currency. Against the dollar, the picture is more balanced: a Federal Reserve that shows little appetite to cut quickly caps sterling's upside, while a Bank of England that looks unlikely to ease further provides a reasonable floor. The next real swing factor is how UK inflation tracks relative to its major peers over the coming months.
currencies.watchToday: The Lloyds House Price Index for July and UK construction PMI are due today, both typically minor movers for sterling. With no Bank of England meeting this week, the bigger tests come from Friday's US non-farm payrolls report and how it shapes Fed expectations.

currencies.headline: Euro holds a tight range as attention turns to today's retail sales and the ECB's latest bulletin.
currencies.commentary:
The euro has traded quietly overnight, with little independent momentum either way. The bigger recent talking point has been July's flash inflation print, where core price growth came in firmer than expected, narrowing the European Central Bank's room to consider further easing even as growth across the bloc remains lacklustre. Today brings the ECB's regular Economic Bulletin along with eurozone retail sales for June, the latter expected to show a meaningful pickup in consumer spending after a soft prior reading, which would offer some reassurance on the domestic demand side of the ECB's outlook.

The single currency continues to look more like a bystander to the dollar's swings than a currency with strong direction of its own, with the ECB now firmly on hold and offering few fresh signals to trade around. Against sterling, the euro remains under pressure from a persistent and wide policy rate gap that continues to favour the pound, while against the dollar its fortunes are tied largely to how quickly the US labour market cools and whether that shifts Federal Reserve expectations. Firmer core inflation gives the ECB less room to manoeuvre should the growth picture deteriorate further.
currencies.watchToday: Eurozone retail sales for June and the ECB's Economic Bulletin are due today, alongside a light broader eurozone calendar. Markets will watch retail sales closely for confirmation that consumer demand is picking up after May's weaker reading, with German industrial production the next notable release later this week.

currencies.headline: Dollar mixed as softer labour market signals collide with a still-divided Fed ahead of Friday's payrolls.
currencies.commentary:
The dollar has traded without a clear direction overnight, caught between two competing narratives. On one hand, this week's data has leaned soft: Wednesday's ADP employment report undershot expectations by a wide margin, and the ISM Services survey also missed, with its employment component dropping sharply, both reinforcing the sense that the US labour market is losing momentum heading into Friday's non-farm payrolls report. On the other hand, July's FOMC minutes revealed an unusually hawkish three-way dissent in favour of higher rates, a reminder that not all policymakers are convinced the case for easing is settled.

That tension defines the dollar's current range-bound behaviour: traders are reluctant to push it decisively lower on cooling data alone while a vocal hawkish minority on the committee remains active, yet equally unwilling to bid it higher given the accumulating signs of labour market softness. Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh's decision to step back from explicit forward guidance has left markets reacting more sharply to each individual data point rather than trading off a clear policy roadmap, a dynamic that is likely to persist through Friday's jobs report and beyond.
currencies.watchToday: A busy US calendar today includes Fed Governor Lisa Cook's speech on the economic outlook, second-quarter productivity data, weekly jobless claims, wholesale inventories, and an evening speech from St. Louis Fed President Alberto Musalem. All of it sets the stage for Friday's non-farm payrolls report, the week's key event.

currencies.headline: Yen extends its recovery for a third session as coordinated support talk keeps markets on alert.
currencies.commentary:
The yen has firmed for a third consecutive session, clawing back some of the ground lost when it slid to a fresh multi-decade low last month. The rebound follows signals of coordinated support from US and Japanese authorities, with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Japanese officials both indicating a willingness to act jointly to steady the currency, keeping markets alert for the possibility of further intervention should the yen resume its slide. The Bank of Japan's decision to hold rates on 31 July, alongside a downward revision to its inflation forecasts, had done little to help the currency in the weeks prior.

The yen's underlying weakness has been driven largely by a wide and persistent gap between US and Japanese bond yields, which continued to widen through late July as markets leaned toward the view that the Bank of Japan's pace of policy normalisation, roughly two rate hikes a year, is too gradual to meaningfully narrow that differential. Today's wage and household spending data will be watched closely, since sustained wage growth remains the key input the Bank of Japan needs to see before it can justify a faster pace of tightening, and by extension before the yen can find more durable support.
currencies.watchToday: Japan's average cash earnings and household spending data for June are due today, a key input for the Bank of Japan's wage-led inflation thesis following its July hold. Beyond today, markets remain watchful for any further signs of official intervention should the yen's recent recovery falter.

currencies.headline: Franc softer against the dollar even as underlying safe-haven demand keeps the SNB on watch.
currencies.commentary:
The Swiss franc has traded on a softer footing against the dollar recently, tracking the broader improvement in risk appetite that has reduced some of the safe-haven demand that supported it earlier in the year. Swiss inflation eased further in July to its lowest reading in four months, reinforcing the Swiss National Bank's comfort with holding its policy rate at zero through the rest of the year. Economists broadly see the SNB's first hike arriving no earlier than 2028, even as some pricing in swap markets creeps toward an earlier move.

The more persistent theme for the franc remains its trade-weighted strength rather than its performance against the dollar specifically: the SNB has repeatedly signalled it stands ready to intervene in currency markets should renewed safe-haven flows push the franc uncomfortably higher against the euro and other trading partners, a stance that has kept a lid on any sustained franc rally. Today's Swiss unemployment data will be watched for further signs of strain in the export sector, which has been feeling the pinch from a strong currency and soft external demand, a dynamic that would only reinforce the case for the SNB to keep policy loose at its September meeting.
currencies.watchToday: Switzerland's unemployment rate for July is due today, with the jobless rate having drifted higher through the year as the export sector strains under a strong currency. The SNB's next policy meeting is not until September, so the franc is likely to keep trading mainly on broader risk sentiment until then.

currencies.headline: Loonie on the back foot after oil's sharp slide, with no domestic data due today.
currencies.commentary:
The Canadian dollar has stayed on the defensive after oil prices tumbled sharply earlier this week, weighed down by comments from Qatari and US officials that raised hopes for a diplomatic resolution to regional tensions. As one of the world's largest oil exporters, Canada's currency remains highly sensitive to swings in crude, and the scale of this week's decline has been enough to outweigh any other domestic considerations for the loonie, with the currency essentially trading as a proxy for the oil market's own risk appetite.

With no Canadian economic data due today, the currency is likely to continue taking its cue almost entirely from the energy complex and broader risk sentiment. A further easing in Middle East tensions would likely extend oil's slide and keep the loonie under pressure, while any renewed flare-up in geopolitical risk could quickly reverse both moves. That sensitivity leaves the Canadian dollar more exposed than most of its peers to headline-driven swings this week, a dynamic worth bearing in mind for anyone with near-term Canadian dollar exposure.
currencies.watchToday: No Canadian economic data is due today, leaving the loonie to trade primarily on oil prices and broader risk sentiment. Markets will continue watching for any developments on Middle East diplomacy that could extend or reverse this week's slide in crude.

currencies.headline: Kiwi holds near recent highs as markets price in further RBNZ tightening next month.
currencies.commentary:
The New Zealand dollar has held close to its best levels in two months, extending the gains that followed the Reserve Bank of New Zealand's decision in July to raise rates for the first time in three years. That move came in response to annual inflation accelerating to 4.1% in the second quarter, above both market expectations and the RBNZ's own forecast, and markets are now almost fully pricing in a further quarter-point hike at the central bank's September meeting. That hawkish repricing has been the single biggest driver of the kiwi's recent outperformance against most major peers.

Beyond the immediate rate story, strategists point to improving domestic sentiment, with New Zealand businesses and consumers turning more optimistic, as a further support for the currency, reinforcing the case that this is a broad-based improvement rather than a one-off reaction to a single data point. Today's RBNZ inflation expectations survey will be watched closely as a fresh gauge of whether businesses and forecasters see price pressures continuing to build, since a further rise would only strengthen the case for the additional tightening markets are already anticipating.
currencies.watchToday: The RBNZ's quarterly inflation expectations survey is due today, watched for signs that businesses and forecasters see price pressures building further, which would reinforce bets on a September rate hike. Beyond today, the RBNZ's 23 September decision remains the next major event for the currency.

currencies.headline: Aussie caught between supportive domestic rates and a still-uneven Chinese recovery.
currencies.commentary:
The Australian dollar remains caught between two competing forces this morning. On the domestic side, the Reserve Bank of Australia's policy settings are seen as broadly supportive, with markets assigning a modest but real chance of a rate hike at its upcoming meeting and a better-than-even probability of one by year end. On the external side, China's recovery continues to look uneven, with industrial production holding up reasonably well while retail sales growth has been notably soft and fixed-asset investment has actually contracted over the first half of the year, a combination that creates a persistent headwind for a currency so tied to Chinese commodity demand.

That tug-of-war between supportive domestic policy and a hesitant Chinese backdrop is likely to keep the Aussie range-bound rather than trending strongly in either direction. Today's trade balance data will be watched closely given China's status as Australia's largest trading partner, with a wider surplus generally read as supportive for the currency. Iron ore demand remains the key channel through which Chinese conditions feed into the Australian dollar, and until China's industrial and investment data show more consistent improvement, the currency is likely to remain sensitive to every incremental data point out of Beijing.
currencies.watchToday: Australia's June trade balance is due today, watched closely for signs of Chinese demand given China's role as Australia's largest trading partner. The Reserve Bank of Australia's next policy decision on 11 August is the bigger event further out, with markets currently split on the odds of a hike.

currencies.headline: Yuan steady near its firmest levels in years as PBoC guidance continues to favour gradual strength.
currencies.commentary:
The offshore yuan has traded steadily, holding near its strongest levels against the dollar in well over a year. The People's Bank of China's daily reference rate has continued to signal comfort with gradual currency strength rather than either a rapid appreciation or a return to weakness, a pattern that has held consistently in recent sessions. Adding to the supportive backdrop, China successfully sold long-dated offshore bonds in Hong Kong at record-low yields this week, reflecting strong global investor demand for Chinese debt and reinforcing confidence in the broader policy environment.

Analysts continue to expect a moderate pace of yuan appreciation through August, citing the potential for further dollar softness, resilient Chinese export performance, and a consistently firm midpoint fixing from the PBoC as the key supports. Policymakers have also reiterated their intent to strengthen Shanghai's role in cross-border finance and reinforce Hong Kong's position as the leading offshore yuan hub, part of a longer-term push to internationalise the currency. With no major Chinese data due today, the currency is likely to keep trading on this same steady, well-managed drift rather than any fresh domestic catalyst.
currencies.watchToday: No major Chinese data is scheduled for today, so the yuan is likely to continue trading on the PBoC's daily fixing and broader risk sentiment. Markets will look ahead to the next trade balance release later this month for a fresh read on export resilience.

currencies.headline: Rand extends its recovery from last month's lows as falling oil prices ease import cost pressures.
currencies.commentary:
The South African rand has continued to claw back ground from the more than three-month low it touched in late July, helped along by this week's sharp slide in oil prices. As a significant net importer of energy, South Africa benefits directly when crude prices fall, both through lower import costs and reduced upward pressure on domestic inflation, and that dynamic has been the primary driver behind the rand's steadier tone over the past week rather than any improvement in the currency's domestic fundamentals.

Those domestic fundamentals remain genuinely mixed: annual inflation accelerated to a two-year high in June, comfortably above the upper end of the South African Reserve Bank's target range, yet the central bank still opted to hold rates at its July meeting in a split decision, with two of six committee members preferring a hike. That combination of elevated inflation and a central bank reluctant to tighten further leaves the rand's recent recovery looking more a function of favourable external conditions, cheaper oil and improved global risk appetite, than any genuine resolution of its underlying vulnerabilities, particularly with August historically one of the weaker months of the year for the currency.
currencies.watchToday: No South African economic data is due today, and the calendar remains light for the rest of the week. With the SARB's next meeting still some weeks away, the rand is likely to keep trading mainly on oil prices and broader global risk sentiment.

currencies.headline: Sterling ticks higher as broad dollar softness offsets a quiet UK data day.
currencies.commentary:
This morning's Lloyds house price data and UK construction PMI reading passed without much fanfare, and sterling has taken its afternoon direction largely from developments elsewhere. A run of soft US data has left the dollar broadly on the back foot into the European afternoon, and sterling has firmed modestly against it as a result. Against the euro, the pound has held a tight range, with little to separate the two currencies since this morning's update.

The bigger story remains the interest rate gap between the Bank of England and its peers, which continues to underpin sterling even without fresh domestic news today.
