With the Bank of Japan and Federal Reserve now moving in less divergent directions than earlier this year, the yen looks better supported than it has in months, though the durability of the move will depend on whether the Bank follows through with an actual hike at a coming meeting.
currencies.watchToday: No major Japanese data is due today. Attention stays on any follow-through from Friday's Bank of Japan decision and the reported intervention, with Wednesday's release of the Bank's June meeting minutes offering a further look at how close the Board came to hiking before this month's hawkish dissent.

currencies.headline: Franc holds its safe-haven bid as Middle East tensions keep demand for havens elevated.
currencies.commentary:
The Swiss franc has traded firmly overnight and into this morning, benefiting from its traditional role as a haven at a time when the latest flare-up in Middle East hostilities has kept broader risk sentiment cautious. The Swiss National Bank has held its policy rate at zero since June and has repeatedly signalled a willingness to intervene in currency markets should franc strength become excessive, but with inflation running at just 0.5% year on year and forecast to peak below 1%, there is little domestic pressure on the Bank to act. Today's July CPI print, due this morning, is one of the few scheduled pieces of Swiss data before the SNB's next quarterly decision in September.

The broader context matters here: Switzerland's comparatively stable economic and political backdrop, combined with elevated global debt levels and recurring geopolitical shocks, continues to funnel safe-haven flows into the franc, even though the SNB has downgraded its 2026 growth forecast to just under 1% on the back of higher US tariffs. That combination of low inflation, a patient central bank, and persistent haven demand leaves the franc structurally well supported, even if a cyclical recovery in Europe could take some of the edge off its strength later in the year.
currencies.watchToday: Swiss CPI for July, released this morning, is the main scheduled event and will feed directly into the SNB's assessment ahead of its September meeting. Beyond today, the calendar is thin for the franc this week, so haven flows tied to the Middle East situation are likely to remain the dominant driver.

currencies.headline: Loonie firmer as the latest jump in oil prices offsets a cautious growth backdrop.
currencies.commentary:
The Canadian dollar has firmed modestly this morning, supported by the recent surge in crude prices after Iran and Israel traded strikes over the weekend, which has added a fresh risk premium to oil markets. That comes on the back of last week's surprisingly strong GDP data, with output rising 0.3% in May against an initial estimate of just 0.1%, and an advance estimate putting annualised second quarter growth at a robust 3.4%, a sharp rebound from the first quarter's mild contraction. The Bank of Canada has no meeting scheduled until early September, leaving the currency to trade mainly on oil and on the broader US dollar backdrop for now.

The connection between oil and the loonie is not always straightforward, but higher crude prices do tend to support Canada's terms of trade even as they add to domestic inflation through higher pump prices and refinery margins, a genuine two-sided effect the Bank of Canada has flagged explicitly in its recent policy communication. With growth data running hotter than expected and oil providing a tailwind, the currency looks reasonably well supported heading into a week where trade figures, rather than any central bank decision, will be the main domestic release.
currencies.watchToday: No major Canadian data is scheduled today. The week's key release is Tuesday's merchandise trade balance for June, watched as a barometer of cross-border demand and tariff related trade frictions, with the Bank of Canada not due to meet again until early September.

currencies.headline: Kiwi firm on hawkish RBNZ signals as traders await a critical labour market test.
currencies.commentary:
The New Zealand dollar has held a firm tone into this morning's session, extending gains built up over the past few weeks after the Reserve Bank of New Zealand delivered its first rate hike in three years at its July meeting. That move followed a hotter than expected inflation print, with annual CPI accelerating to 4.1% in the second quarter, above both the 4.0% consensus and the Bank's own 3.9% forecast, and markets now widely expect a further hike at the September meeting. There is no major New Zealand data due today, so the currency continues to trade largely on that hawkish RBNZ narrative alongside the broader risk backdrop shaped by Middle East developments and the US dollar.

The stakes are rising heading into tomorrow: strategists have pointed to above-target inflation and an improving domestic growth outlook as the key supports for further RBNZ tightening, but that view rests heavily on the labour market holding up. A weak reading tomorrow would raise real questions about how much further the Bank can realistically tighten without denting employment, making it arguably the single most important release for the currency this week.
currencies.watchToday: No major New Zealand data is due today. The week's pivotal release is tomorrow's second quarter employment and unemployment report, which lands just weeks after the RBNZ's hawkish pivot and will be watched closely for signs of whether the labour market can withstand further tightening.

currencies.headline: Aussie caught between a supportive RBA stance and an uneven Chinese recovery.
currencies.commentary:
The Australian dollar has traded steadily this morning, caught between two competing forces that have defined its recent path. On one hand, the Reserve Bank of Australia has held its cash rate in a wait-and-see stance, with markets pricing only around a one in four chance of a hike at its next meeting but better than even odds of one by year end, a supportive backdrop for the currency. On the other, China's official manufacturing PMI slipped back into contraction at 49.2 in July, well below the 50.0 consensus, and broader Chinese activity data showed retail sales growth slowing to just 1.0% year on year and fixed asset investment falling 5.7% in the first half, a genuine headwind for a currency so tied to commodity demand.

The mechanism linking the two matters directly for the Aussie: China remains Australia's largest trading partner and the main buyer of its iron ore and other commodity exports, so a cooling Chinese economy weighs on Australia's terms of trade even as domestic interest rate settings stay relatively supportive. That tug of war between a patient RBA and an uneven Chinese recovery is likely to keep the currency choppy and headline-driven, with Chinese data proving just as important to the Aussie's path as anything released domestically.
currencies.watchToday: No major Australian data is due today, though this morning's China Caixin manufacturing PMI, a private-sector gauge watched closely for its trade linkages to Australia, is relevant background after the weaker official Chinese PMI on Friday. The week's key domestic release is Thursday's trade balance, watched closely given China's outsized role as a buyer of Australian exports.

currencies.headline: Yuan steady as Beijing pushes ahead with reforms even as factory activity data sends mixed signals.
currencies.commentary:
The offshore yuan has traded in a tight, well contained range this morning, consistent with its recent pattern of stability even as the currency has been one of the better performers among major currencies so far in 2026. That stability comes despite a mixed picture on the factory floor: the official NBS manufacturing PMI slipped back into contraction at 49.2 in July, below the 50.0 consensus, while this morning's private sector Caixin manufacturing PMI, which tends to skew toward smaller export and tech oriented firms, offers a cross-check on whether that weakness is broad based. The People's Bank of China has continued to strike a supportive but cautious tone, with Governor Pan Gongsheng highlighting broadening international demand for the yuan without signalling any imminent shift in rates.

The bigger story is structural rather than cyclical: Beijing has been rolling out measures to cement Hong Kong's role as the main offshore hub for the yuan, including higher caps on cross-border trading and bond connect schemes, a long-term push toward internationalising the currency that sits somewhat apart from the near-term factory data. For now, that structural support and the PBoC's steady hand are keeping the yuan anchored within a well defined band, even as the divergence between the official and private manufacturing surveys leaves some uncertainty about the true state of Chinese industrial demand, a point with knock-on relevance for commodity currencies like the Australian and New Zealand dollars.
currencies.watchToday: This morning's Caixin manufacturing PMI for July is the main release, watched as a cross-check on Friday's weaker official NBS PMI reading, with the Caixin services PMI following on Wednesday. Beyond the data, the PBoC's ongoing structural reforms around Hong Kong's offshore yuan market remain the bigger medium-term theme for the currency.

currencies.headline: Rand steady as the SARB's surprise hold and rising inflation set a cautious tone.
currencies.commentary:
The South African rand has traded with a steady tone this morning, digesting last week's surprise decision by the South African Reserve Bank to leave its policy rate unchanged in a split 4-2 vote, a move markets had not fully priced in. That hold came even as annual inflation accelerated to 5.0% in June, the highest reading in two years and above the 4.7% consensus, driven mainly by transport and housing costs, leaving the Bank in a genuinely delicate position between supporting growth and containing price pressures. This morning's Absa/BER manufacturing PMI for July is the first data point of the new week and will give an early read on the health of the sector.

Governor Lesetja Kganyago used last Friday's Reserve Bank annual meeting to reaffirm the Bank's commitment to its new 3% inflation target while also warning that renewed conflict in the Middle East could add further inflation risk through higher oil and fertiliser prices, a reminder that global shocks are feeding directly into South Africa's domestic price outlook. With the SARB's next policy meeting not due until September, the rand is likely to keep trading on that inflation and global risk narrative, alongside broader dollar sentiment, rather than on any fresh domestic catalyst this week.
currencies.watchToday: The Absa/BER manufacturing PMI for July, due this morning, is today's only scheduled release and will offer an early signal on the sector's health. With the SARB not meeting again until September, the rand is likely to keep trading on last week's inflation surprise and on broader global risk sentiment, including any further escalation in the Middle East, for the rest of the week.

currencies.headline: Sterling shrugs off a much weaker UK factory PMI as broad dollar softness lends support.
currencies.commentary:
This morning's final UK manufacturing PMI landed well below expectations, revised down to a four month low as new order growth and hiring both cooled, a notably weaker outcome than the earlier flash estimate had suggested. On its own that would typically weigh on sterling, but the currency has instead traded with a firmer tone through the European afternoon, helped by the broader retreat in the dollar that followed confirmation of the joint US Japan intervention to support the yen. Cable has pushed toward its best level in a couple of weeks even as the domestic data disappointed, a reminder that external forces are currently doing more to move the pound than anything happening at home.

That divergence between soft UK data and a firmer pound says as much about the dollar's troubles as it does about British fundamentals. With the Bank of England on hold and no meeting scheduled this week, sterling is effectively trading as a proxy for dollar sentiment, and today's weak PMI print raises a small question mark over the strength of the recovery in UK manufacturing heading into Wednesday's services reading, which will offer a fuller picture of the domestic economy.
currencies.watchToday: Nothing further is scheduled for sterling specifically for the rest of today; the next data point lands just after midnight with the BRC shop price and retail sales monitors for July. The bigger test comes Wednesday with the UK's final services PMI, while this afternoon's US ISM manufacturing print is likely to matter more for cable in the short term than anything on the domestic calendar.

currencies.headline: Euro extends its advance as a firm PMI confirmation meets a broadly weaker dollar.
currencies.commentary:
This morning's final eurozone manufacturing PMI was confirmed a touch below the earlier flash estimate but still at its strongest reading since April, with German factory output reported at a four year high. That modestly encouraging confirmation has been overshadowed by the bigger story of the session, the broad dollar retreat that followed confirmation of coordinated US Japan intervention to support the yen, which has pushed the euro to its firmest level against the dollar in about six weeks. The single currency has held those gains through the European afternoon with little sign of profit taking so far.

The combination of resilient eurozone factory data and a softer dollar reinforces the case markets built last week for a European Central Bank that stays on hold for longer, after core inflation surprised to the upside. With the ECB's next meeting still some weeks away, the euro's near term path looks more tied to how the dollar story evolves than to fresh eurozone news, at least until Wednesday's services PMI and producer price figures provide the next real test.
currencies.watchToday: No further eurozone data is due for the rest of today. Wednesday brings the final services and composite PMIs alongside producer price figures, with Thursday's retail sales rounding out the week's releases, all of which will help confirm whether last week's hawkish inflation surprise has further to run.

currencies.headline: Dollar slips back as confirmation of the weekend's yen intervention overshadows this morning's steadier tone.
currencies.commentary:
The dollar has given back this morning's modest steadiness through the European afternoon, turning softer again as Japan's Finance Ministry and the US Treasury formally confirmed last week's coordinated intervention to support the yen, the first joint action of its kind since 2011. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent reinforced the move by warning that Washington would not hesitate to join further coordinated action if needed, comments that have kept the dollar under broad pressure rather than just against the yen, with the euro and sterling both firmer as a result and Asian currencies mixed as markets digest the shift.

The bigger question for the dollar this afternoon is whether it can find its footing once the ISM manufacturing survey lands later today, the first major US data point of a week that builds toward Friday's payrolls report. A stronger than expected reading could help the currency stabilise after a rough stretch, while a miss would likely compound today's intervention driven weakness. Markets are also weighing what the renewed willingness to intervene signals about the administration's tolerance for further dollar declines.
currencies.watchToday: The US ISM manufacturing PMI for July, due this afternoon, is the key remaining release, with markets looking for an improvement on June's reading and watching the prices paid and new orders components closely. It kicks off a data heavy week that builds toward Wednesday's ISM services PMI and Fed minutes, and Friday's non farm payrolls.

currencies.headline: Yen holds the bulk of its intervention driven surge as Tokyo signals readiness to act again.
currencies.commentary:
The yen has held onto most of its recent sharp advance through the European afternoon, having jumped to its strongest level in around three months after Japan's Finance Ministry and the US Treasury confirmed last week's coordinated intervention to support the currency. Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama told reporters today that the authorities would not hesitate to act again, while Treasury Secretary Bessent backed the operation as a response to disorderly moves, comments that have helped the currency defend its gains through the session rather than drift back toward the multi decade lows hit before the intervention.

This marks the first coordinated US Japan intervention since 2011 and reflects growing discomfort in Washington as well as Tokyo with how far the yen had fallen, given the currency's slide to levels not seen since the 1980s and the knock on effect on the US trade deficit. With both sides now on record as willing to intervene again, the bar for a fresh bout of sharp yen weakness looks meaningfully higher than it did a week ago, even if the underlying interest rate gap that drove the decline remains largely intact.
currencies.watchToday: No Japanese data is due for the rest of today. Wednesday's release of the Bank of Japan's June meeting minutes is the next scheduled catalyst, offering a further look at how close the board came to raising rates before this month's hawkish dissent, though fresh intervention headlines remain the more immediate risk in either direction.

currencies.headline: Franc holds firm as a softer inflation print and a cautious risk mood reinforce its haven bid.
currencies.commentary:
Swiss inflation data released this morning came in softer than expected, with the annual rate easing from June's reading as fuel prices and airfares fell, while core inflation held steady. That undershoot has done nothing to dent the franc, which has instead traded firmly through the European afternoon alongside the yen as investors lean into haven currencies amid a genuinely unsettled session, with Asian equities mixed to sharply lower after the dollar's intervention driven wobble and South Korea's benchmark index posting a particularly steep decline overnight.

The soft inflation print further reduces any near term pressure on the Swiss National Bank to act, whether through rate changes or currency intervention, since price growth remains comfortably contained well below the levels troubling other major economies. With the SNB's next policy decision not due until September, the franc's path from here looks tied more to how broader risk sentiment and the dollar story evolve than to anything happening domestically.
currencies.watchToday: No further Swiss data is scheduled for the rest of today, and the calendar stays quiet for the franc through the rest of the week. Haven demand tied to the broader market mood, along with any follow through from today's yen intervention headlines, remains the more likely driver into tomorrow.

currencies.headline: Loonie gives back its morning gains as oil reverses sharply on ceasefire relief.
currencies.commentary:
The Canadian dollar has turned softer through the European afternoon, unwinding the gains it made earlier in the session when crude prices spiked on reports of Iran and Israel trading strikes over the weekend. That early oil driven strength has reversed hard as signs the ceasefire is holding and Iranian barrels returning to the market have pulled crude sharply lower, with West Texas Intermediate giving back a large chunk of its recent advance. Since Canada remains one of the world's most oil sensitive currencies, the loonie has moved almost in lockstep with the swing in crude.

The round trip in oil prices, up sharply overnight then down just as sharply this afternoon, highlights how exposed the currency remains to swings in Middle East headlines even as the domestic backdrop stays relatively settled. Last week's stronger than expected GDP data and the Bank of Canada's more neutral tone have taken a back seat for now, with the currency likely to keep trading as a function of the oil market and geopolitical headlines rather than anything on the local calendar until tomorrow.
currencies.watchToday: No Canadian data is due for the rest of today. Tomorrow's merchandise trade balance for June is the next scheduled release and will be watched as a barometer of cross border demand, though oil prices and the durability of the Middle East ceasefire remain the dominant near term drivers.

currencies.headline: Kiwi holds its recent gains as broad dollar weakness adds to an already hawkish RBNZ backdrop.
currencies.commentary:
The New Zealand dollar has had a quiet but firm afternoon, with little fresh domestic news landing since this morning, extending the steady tone it has held since last month's stronger than expected inflation print and the Reserve Bank's first rate hike in three years. The broader retreat in the dollar following the confirmed US Japan yen intervention has added a modest extra tailwind, lifting most major currencies against the greenback simultaneously rather than reflecting anything specific to New Zealand.

With no domestic data due until tomorrow, the kiwi's next real test comes from the labour market rather than from today's session. Markets are already positioning for the possibility of another quarter point hike in September, and tomorrow's employment report will be the clearest signal yet of whether the jobs market can withstand further tightening without cracking, making it a considerably bigger event for the currency than anything left on today's calendar.
currencies.watchToday: New Zealand's second quarter employment and unemployment report, due late tomorrow evening UK time, is a high importance release and the clearest test yet of how the labour market is holding up under RBNZ tightening. Beyond that, broader risk sentiment and any further fallout from today's dollar weakness remain the other swing factors into tomorrow.

currencies.headline: Aussie stays capped by a soft Chinese PMI and a shaky regional equity mood despite the weaker dollar.
currencies.commentary:
The Australian dollar has struggled to fully capitalise on the broader dollar weakness this afternoon, held back by a private sector Chinese manufacturing survey published this morning that missed expectations and eased to its softest reading in several months, adding to Friday's disappointing official Chinese PMI. Asian equity markets were mixed to sharply lower overnight as the region digested the confirmed US Japan intervention, with South Korea's index tumbling more than five percent, and that cautious regional mood has left the Aussie trading in a narrow range rather than joining sterling and the euro in pushing meaningfully higher against the dollar.

The combination underlines how much the Australian dollar behaves as a proxy for Chinese growth sentiment, with two soft factory readings in the space of a few trading days reinforcing concerns about the health of its largest trading partner even as the Reserve Bank of Australia maintains a cautiously supportive stance. That tension between a resilient domestic policy backdrop and a wobblier China story looks set to keep the currency rangebound until fresh catalysts emerge.
currencies.watchToday: No Australian data is due for the rest of today. Thursday's trade balance is the next domestic release, though China's trade figures on Friday are likely to carry more weight for the Aussie given the size of the trading relationship.

currencies.headline: Yuan steady as a soft private sector PMI adds to Friday's weak official reading.
currencies.commentary:
A private sector gauge of Chinese manufacturing activity published this morning missed expectations and eased to its softest level in several months, though it stayed just above the growth threshold, adding to Friday's weaker official reading and reinforcing a picture of cooling momentum in China's factory sector. The offshore yuan has nonetheless remained well contained through the afternoon, with the People's Bank of China again setting its daily reference rate on the weaker side of where the market had expected, consistent with its recent pattern of leaning against further currency appreciation even as the dollar broadly retreats elsewhere.

The back to back soft PMI prints, official and private sector alike, sit somewhat awkwardly against the yuan's status as one of the better performing major currencies so far this year, and will likely feed into questions about whether Beijing needs to lean harder on stimulus to support growth. For now the central bank's tight grip on the daily fixing continues to keep the currency's day to day moves unusually contained regardless of what the underlying data shows.
currencies.watchToday: Nothing further is scheduled for the yuan for the rest of today. Wednesday's private sector services PMI is the next release, followed by Friday's trade balance figures, which will offer a fuller read on how external demand is holding up.

currencies.headline: Rand fails to fully ride the dollar's slide as risk-off cross-currents and seasonal caution weigh.
currencies.commentary:
This morning's Absa manufacturing PMI for July pointed to continued softness in South Africa's factory sector, extending a run of weak readings and offering little in the way of positive surprise. The rand has struggled to draw much lasting support from the broader dollar weakness that has lifted most other majors this afternoon following the confirmed US Japan intervention, with the currency's gains proving more muted than sterling's or the euro's as the cautious mood in Asian equity markets bleeds into risk appetite for emerging market currencies more broadly.

That relative underperformance fits a broader pattern for the rand, which enters August, historically its weakest month, still digesting last month's surprise decision by the Reserve Bank to leave rates unchanged despite inflation running at a two year high, and recent reports of foreign investors turning net sellers of local bonds. With domestic policy on hold until September, the currency looks more exposed than most to any wobble in broader risk appetite over the coming weeks.
currencies.watchToday: No further South African data is scheduled for the rest of today, and the calendar stays quiet for the rand through the rest of the week. Broader dollar sentiment and global risk appetite, rather than anything domestic, are likely to remain the main drivers into tomorrow.

currencies.headline: Sterling stays on the back foot as fiscal jitters overshadow yesterday's steady Bank of England hold.
currencies.commentary:
The pound has drifted lower overnight and into this morning, extending a pullback that began earlier in the week as gilt yields sit near multi-month highs. Yesterday's Bank of England decision, a widely expected hold at 3.75% for a fifth straight meeting, did little to change the picture, with focus instead on the government's search for flexibility within its fiscal rules ahead of the autumn budget. That fiscal uncertainty, rather than anything from the Bank, has been the dominant driver of sterling sentiment this week.

The mechanism here matters: rising gilt yields reflect investors demanding a bigger premium to hold UK government debt amid spending uncertainty, and that risk premium has been weighing on the currency even though higher yields would normally support it. Until the government's fiscal plans are clarified, likely not before the October budget, relief rallies in both gilts and the pound are likely to stay capped, leaving sterling more exposed to fiscal headlines than to the usual interest rate story for now.
currencies.watchToday: No UK data is scheduled for today. The week ahead brings only lower-tier releases: manufacturing PMI on Monday, construction PMI on Tuesday and services PMI on Wednesday, so sterling is likely to keep trading on fiscal policy headlines and broader gilt market moves rather than fresh data.

currencies.headline: Euro treads carefully into today's flash inflation data after yesterday's upside growth surprise.
currencies.commentary:
The euro has been broadly steady this morning as traders position for two closely watched releases due later today: the Eurozone flash CPI print for July and the flash unemployment rate. That follows yesterday's Q2 GDP flash estimate, which came in well ahead of forecasts and eased fears the bloc might post a second weak quarter in a row, with Germany's own growth figure also beating expectations. The single currency firmed modestly on that data but has since settled into a narrower range ahead of today's inflation numbers.

Today's CPI print carries more weight than usual: economists expect the annual rate to rebound from June's 2.8%, largely on higher energy costs tied to the Middle East conflict, while core inflation is seen holding closer to 2.4%. A hotter than expected headline number would complicate the ECB's task, adding pressure to keep policy tight even as growth remains fragile, a combination that has historically supported the euro in the near term but raises longer run concerns about the health of the recovery.
currencies.watchToday: Eurozone flash CPI for July and the unemployment rate are both due at 10:00 UK time today, the key releases of the week for the euro. A hot inflation surprise would reinforce the case for the ECB to stay cautious on rate cuts, while a soft print would ease that pressure; ECB speakers through the rest of the week will be watched for reaction.

currencies.headline: Dollar holds firm as markets digest a surprisingly hawkish set of Fed dissents.
currencies.commentary:
The dollar remains broadly well supported this morning, building on its recovery from a multi-year low earlier this month. Wednesday's Federal Reserve decision saw the Committee hold rates steady, but three regional presidents dissented in favour of higher rates, the first time since 2016 that a trio of policymakers has pushed collectively in the same direction given inflation that has now run above target for more than five years. That unusual show of hawkishness has lifted Treasury yields and pulled forward market pricing for a possible move as soon as September.

The shift matters because it changes the market's read on the Fed's reaction function: rather than simply holding until inflation cools further, a meaningful minority of the Committee now appears willing to tighten further if price pressures persist. That has been the dominant force behind the dollar's rebound this month, outweighing periodic bouts of safe haven demand and unwind tied to the Middle East conflict. With today's calendar light, the dollar is likely to keep taking its cues from Fed pricing and Treasury yields rather than fresh data.
currencies.watchToday: Only the Chicago PMI, a lower-tier regional survey, is due for the US today. With no major releases scheduled, the dollar is likely to keep trading on the fallout from Wednesday's Fed decision and shifting rate hike expectations heading into September.

currencies.headline: Yen swings sharply as the Bank of Japan holds but signals a firmer path toward the next hike.
currencies.commentary:
The yen has been the most volatile of the majors overnight, rallying hard after sliding to its weakest level against the dollar in roughly four decades earlier in the week. Tokyo and US authorities intervened directly on Thursday night to slow the currency's slide, and this morning's Tokyo core CPI print added to the momentum, accelerating to 1.9% year on year and beating forecasts. The Bank of Japan then held its policy rate at 1.00% as widely expected, though one board member dissented in favour of an immediate hike, and the accompanying Outlook Report flagged inflation likely running clearly above the 2% target from later this fiscal year.

Governor Ueda's press conference this morning reinforced that message, with board members reportedly seeing risks to their inflation forecasts skewed to the upside and Ueda signalling readiness to raise rates further if growth and prices track as expected. That combination, direct intervention plus a central bank leaning more hawkish, is a meaningful shift after months of the yen drifting weaker on the gap between Japanese and US rates, and puts the timing of the next hike, whether October or December, firmly in focus for the rest of the year.
currencies.watchToday: Tokyo's core CPI, the Bank of Japan's rate decision and Governor Ueda's press conference were all released earlier this morning and are the key events driving today's session. With those now in hand, attention turns to next week's national CPI print for confirmation of today's inflation and policy signals.

currencies.headline: Franc drifts lower as the SNB's zero rate policy widens its gap with a still-restrictive Fed.
currencies.commentary:
The franc has softened modestly overnight, extending a gradual decline this week as the policy gap between the Swiss National Bank's zero percent rate and a Federal Reserve still holding well above 3% continues to work against the currency. That drift lower comes despite a genuinely upbeat domestic data point yesterday, the KOF Economic Barometer for July, a leading indicator that jumped comfortably above forecasts to its best reading since February on broad based improvement across manufacturing, construction and services.

The disconnect between resilient Swiss data and a softer currency illustrates how dominant the rate differential has become for the franc right now: the SNB has downgraded its 2026 growth outlook on the drag from US tariffs, kept inflation forecasts comfortably within its target band, and signalled it is willing to intervene directly in currency markets if the franc were to strengthen too aggressively against the euro. With little prospect of a policy shift from Bern, the franc looks set to keep taking its direction mainly from US rate expectations and broader risk appetite rather than domestic developments.
currencies.watchToday: No Swiss data is due today. The next scheduled catalyst is Monday's Swiss CPI print for July, which will be watched for confirmation that inflation is tracking within the SNB's comfort zone.

currencies.headline: Loonie steadies as oil eases off its Middle East driven highs.
currencies.commentary:
The Canadian dollar has firmed a little overnight after a choppy week in which it briefly touched its softest level in about two weeks against the US dollar as oil prices swung on developments in the Middle East. Brent crude has pulled back from the highs above 92 dollars a barrel it reached earlier this week on fears of a wider US-Iran conflict, easing back below 90 dollars, and that partial unwind of the geopolitical risk premium has taken some pressure off the loonie given Canada's position as a major oil exporter.

The relationship is mechanical: Canada's terms of trade improve when oil rises and worsen when it falls, so CAD tends to track crude prices closely on days when energy markets are moving on their own news rather than broader dollar strength or weakness. With the Bank of Canada's next policy decision still some weeks away, oil and any further developments in the Middle East are likely to remain the more important drivers for the loonie in the near term, with today's domestic growth data a secondary factor.
currencies.watchToday: Canada's GDP by industry report for May, with a June advance estimate, is due this afternoon and will give an early read on how the economy is tracking into the third quarter. Beyond that, oil price moves tied to the Middle East situation remain the dominant driver for CAD this week.

currencies.headline: Kiwi holds gains as hawkish RBNZ signals continue to outweigh global risk aversion.
currencies.commentary:
The New Zealand dollar has traded firmly this morning, building on a recovery through July that has come despite periodic bouts of risk aversion tied to the Middle East conflict. The move follows the Reserve Bank of New Zealand's rate hike earlier this month, which took the Official Cash Rate to 2.50%, and a batch of data since then that has reinforced the hawkish case: annual inflation accelerated to 4.1% in the second quarter, its highest since late 2023, while yesterday's ANZ Business Outlook survey jumped to its strongest reading since February.

Markets are now pricing another quarter point hike in September, with rates seen reaching at least 3.0% by year end, and that repricing has been the main support for the kiwi even as broader risk sentiment has been choppy. The mechanism is straightforward: a central bank hiking into an inflation overshoot tends to draw in yield seeking flows, and New Zealand's is currently one of the more hawkish among major central banks, a contrast that has helped the currency outperform some of its more dovish peers this month.
currencies.watchToday: No NZD data is scheduled for today. The week's key release is Tuesday's employment and unemployment data for the second quarter, which will be watched closely for confirmation that the labour market can withstand further RBNZ tightening.

currencies.headline: Aussie dips as another soft China PMI print weighs on the growth-sensitive currency.
currencies.commentary:
The Australian dollar has eased slightly this morning after China's official manufacturing PMI for July fell back into contraction, dropping to 49.2 from June's 50.3 and missing forecasts, with the non-manufacturing gauge also softening. New orders fell to their lowest level since 2023, a sign that the recent stabilisation in Chinese factory activity has proven short lived. Given China takes a large share of Australian commodity exports, weak readings from its manufacturing sector tend to flow through quickly to sentiment on the Australian dollar.

The transmission mechanism here is direct: softer Chinese industrial activity implies weaker near term demand for the iron ore, coal and other raw materials that underpin a large part of Australia's export income, which in turn weighs on the terms of trade and the currency. That headwind sits alongside a still relatively hawkish Reserve Bank of Australia, which has kept the door open to further tightening given lingering inflation risks, a combination that has left the Aussie somewhat range bound as domestic and external forces pull in different directions.
currencies.watchToday: Australia's producer price index for the second quarter is due this morning, a lower-tier release that the RBA watches for early signs of cost pressures building through supply chains. The bigger driver remains today's China PMI data, already released, with further confirmation due from China's Caixin manufacturing survey on Monday.

currencies.headline: Yuan holds near three-year highs even as factory data disappoints.
currencies.commentary:
The offshore yuan has extended its rally to a fresh three-year high this morning, a striking divergence from today's official PMI data, which showed China's manufacturing sector slipping back into contraction in July with new orders at their weakest since 2023. The currency's strength instead reflects several straight days of the People's Bank of China setting its daily reference rate stronger than expected, a signal that policymakers are comfortable with, or even encouraging, a firmer yuan even as underlying growth momentum cools.

That combination matters because it shows the yuan currently trading more on policy signalling and capital flows than on domestic data surprises: Beijing's Politburo has pledged to step up macroeconomic support and bolster capital market resilience for the rest of the year, and a firmer currency fixing can be read as part of that broader effort to project confidence. At the same time, the PBoC has also nudged its most recent fixings a little weaker than the market expected, suggesting officials want to moderate the pace of gains rather than let the yuan run too far, too fast.
currencies.watchToday: China's official manufacturing and non-manufacturing PMI data for July, both released earlier this morning, are the main scheduled events and came in softer than expected. The Caixin manufacturing PMI, a private sector alternative more focused on smaller exporters, follows on Monday.

currencies.headline: Rand stays under pressure as elevated inflation limits the SARB's room to manoeuvre.
currencies.commentary:
The South African rand remains on the back foot this morning, still digesting the fallout from the Reserve Bank's surprise decision last week to leave its main interest rate unchanged at 7.0% rather than deliver the hike markets had largely expected. That decision, passed on a narrow vote among committee members, left the rand trading near its softest level in several months, with annual inflation having accelerated to 5.0% in June, its highest in two years, and core inflation also picking up.

The mechanism at play is straightforward: when a central bank holds rates steady despite inflation running hot and above target, it effectively lowers the real, inflation adjusted return on holding the currency, which tends to weigh on demand for it. Governor Kganyago has flagged that renewed conflict in the Middle East, and the associated rise in oil and fertiliser prices, could yet force the SARB's hand on further tightening if higher fuel costs feed through to food prices and core inflation, keeping the door open to a shift in stance at the next meeting in September.
currencies.watchToday: Governor Kganyago addresses the SARB's annual general meeting this morning, a speech that will be closely watched for any fresh signals on the path for interest rates ahead of September's Monetary Policy Committee meeting. No hard data is due for ZAR today, so this speech is the main scheduled event.

currencies.headline: Sterling steadies as gilt yields ease back from this week's highs, though fiscal caution lingers.
currencies.commentary:
Since this morning, UK gilt yields have eased back modestly from the highs touched earlier in the week, with the shorter end pulling back more than long-dated debt. That easing has taken a little pressure off sterling's dominant story of the past fortnight. There has been no fresh UK data during the European afternoon session, so the pound has largely been taking its cues from the broader dollar, which has softened noticeably as US equities rallied hard and Treasury yields eased; that backdrop has let sterling firm modestly even as domestic fiscal jitters persist.

The underlying story has not changed: Prime Minister Andy Burnham's government is still working out how much room it has within its fiscal rules ahead of the autumn budget, and investors remain wary of a repeat of the borrowing overshoot seen earlier this fiscal year. Chancellor John Healey's early signals on spending priorities will matter more for sterling over the coming weeks than anything in today's session, so this afternoon's modest recovery should be read as a pause in the fiscal repricing rather than a reversal of it.
currencies.watchToday: No UK data is left on today's calendar. Markets head into the weekend focused on Monday's UK manufacturing PMI, a lower-tier release, with construction and services PMIs following Tuesday and Wednesday; until then sterling is likely to keep tracking gilt market sentiment and the broader dollar.

currencies.headline: Euro ticks higher after flash inflation surprises slightly to the upside on core prices.
currencies.commentary:
The session's key event has now landed: Eurozone flash inflation for July accelerated to an annual pace of 2.9%, up from June's 2.8% and in line with the headline forecast, but core inflation, which strips out food and energy, ticked up to 2.5% versus the 2.4% economists had pencilled in. Energy costs were the biggest driver, with the annual energy inflation rate jumping to 10.0% from 8.5% in June as the Middle East conflict continues to feed through to fuel prices. The euro firmed modestly in the immediate aftermath, extending the gentle strengthening seen since yesterday's upside growth surprise.

The core beat is the more important number for the ECB: a headline print in line with forecasts is easy to look through, but underlying price pressure running slightly hotter than expected reinforces the case for the central bank to stay patient rather than resume cutting rates anytime soon. Combined with yesterday's stronger than expected GDP data, today's numbers paint a picture of an economy holding up better than feared while inflation proves stickier than hoped, a combination that has tended to support the euro this week even as it complicates the growth-inflation trade-off the ECB is trying to manage.
currencies.watchToday: With today's flash CPI now out of the way, there is little else scheduled for the euro this afternoon. Attention shifts into next week, when Monday's final manufacturing PMI readings for Germany and the wider bloc will show whether the sector is stabilising, alongside ECB speakers who will be watched for reaction to today's inflation surprise.

currencies.headline: Dollar broadly softer into the New York open as risk appetite surges and yields ease.
currencies.commentary:
The dollar has lost ground during the European afternoon, giving back some of this week's gains as US equities point to a sharp rally on Wall Street and Treasury yields have edged lower. That is a shift from this morning's tone, when the currency was still drawing support from Wednesday's unusually hawkish trio of Fed dissents; the softer afternoon move looks more about broad risk appetite than about any change in the Fed outlook itself, which remains intact.

Still to come this afternoon are the Chicago PMI and the final University of Michigan consumer sentiment reading for July; the preliminary sentiment print earlier this month jumped by nearly five points to its best level since February on the back of falling petrol prices, so today's final read will show whether that improvement held through the rest of the month. With Fed pricing for a possible move as soon as September still intact, the dollar's near-term direction is likely to keep hinging on that rate story more than on today's second-tier data, even as the softer afternoon tone shows risk sentiment can still push back against it.
currencies.watchToday: Chicago PMI is due at 14:45 UK time, followed by the final University of Michigan consumer sentiment reading at 15:00, both lower-tier releases unlikely to shift the bigger picture on their own. The more important driver into next week remains Fed pricing following Wednesday's hawkish dissents, alongside Monday's ISM manufacturing PMI.

currencies.headline: Yen gives back much of this morning's intervention-driven spike as the session wears on.
currencies.commentary:
The yen has pared a significant chunk of the sharp gains it posted overnight, when suspected intervention by Japanese authorities and a hotter than expected Tokyo inflation print drove one of its strongest rallies in months. Through the European afternoon it has drifted back weaker, unwinding much of that spike even though the Bank of Japan's post-decision message from Governor Ueda was read by strategists as mildly hawkish, with board members reportedly seeing inflation risks skewed to the upside. That the currency is fading the hawkish signal rather than building on it suggests intervention flows, not a genuine repricing of rate expectations, did most of the work overnight.

This is a reminder of how quickly intervention-driven moves can fade once the initial shock wears off: without further concrete signals on timing, whether from Ueda or from renewed direct intervention, the yen looks vulnerable to resuming its underlying downtrend, which has been driven mainly by the wide gap between US and Japanese rates rather than by anything specific to Japan. Markets will be watching closely whether Tokyo's monetary authorities step in again if the currency slides back toward the multi-decade lows touched earlier this week.
currencies.watchToday: With the Bank of Japan decision, Governor Ueda's press conference and this morning's Tokyo inflation data all now behind it, there is nothing further scheduled for the yen today. The next major catalyst is next week's nationwide inflation data, which will show whether Tokyo's upside surprise was a broader trend or a one-off.

currencies.headline: Franc drifts modestly lower as a risk-on mood in equities saps demand for safety.
currencies.commentary:
There has been little Switzerland-specific news since this morning, but the franc has softened slightly further through the European afternoon as a sharp rally in US equity markets and easing Treasury yields have taken some shine off havens more broadly. That is consistent with the pattern seen through the week: the franc has tended to move more on global risk appetite and the gap between Swiss and US interest rates than on domestic developments, and today has been no exception.

The Swiss National Bank's zero percent policy rate continues to leave the franc structurally disadvantaged against a Federal Reserve still holding well above 3%, and with no Swiss data or SNB commentary due before next week, that rate gap is likely to remain the dominant driver into the weekend. Any further pickup in risk appetite, or continued digestion of Wednesday's Fed press conference, could extend the franc's gentle drift lower.
currencies.watchToday: Nothing further is scheduled for the franc today. The next scheduled catalyst is Monday's Swiss CPI print for July, which will be watched for confirmation that inflation is tracking comfortably within the SNB's target band.

currencies.headline: Loonie firms modestly with Canada's May GDP report due imminently.
currencies.commentary:
The Canadian dollar has continued to firm gradually through the session, building on its recovery from the roughly two-week low touched earlier in the week, helped by a broadly softer US dollar and oil prices that have stabilised after this week's swings tied to the Middle East. Statistics Canada's GDP by industry report for May, together with an advance estimate for June, lands in the early afternoon and will offer the first real signal of how the economy performed heading into the second quarter, following two consecutive quarterly contractions.

The Bank of Canada has pencilled in a meaningful rebound in second quarter growth, so today's release matters for whether that expectation still holds. A weak print would revive concerns the economy is struggling to gain traction and could cap the loonie's recent recovery, while a figure closer to the Bank's expectations would reinforce the currency's modest firming trend. Either way, oil remains the more consistent driver for CAD day to day, given Canada's position as a major exporter, and today's partial stabilisation in crude has been a supportive backdrop.
currencies.watchToday: Canada's GDP by industry report for May, with the June advance estimate, is due at 13:30 UK time and is the main scheduled event left today. Beyond that, oil prices and any further Middle East headlines remain the dominant driver for the loonie, with Canada's June merchandise trade balance due next Tuesday.

currencies.headline: Kiwi eases back from its best levels despite an upbeat confidence reading.
currencies.commentary:
The New Zealand dollar has pulled back somewhat from the eight-week highs touched earlier this week, even after a genuinely encouraging domestic data point: the ANZ-Roy Morgan consumer confidence index jumped eight points in July to one of its stronger readings in some time. The pullback instead reflects the drag from this morning's weak Chinese manufacturing PMI, which fell back into contraction and dented sentiment toward China-exposed currencies broadly, New Zealand included given how much of its trade runs through China.

Even with today's pullback, the kiwi remains on track to be one of the better performers among the majors this week, still underpinned by the Reserve Bank of New Zealand's hawkish tilt after this month's rate hike and the accompanying acceleration in inflation to a multi-year high. That contrast, resilient domestic policy support against a wobblier external backdrop from China, is likely to keep the kiwi somewhat two-sided into next week, with the currency's own data taking over as the more important driver once Tuesday's employment figures land.
currencies.watchToday: Nothing further is scheduled for the New Zealand dollar today. The key event for the week ahead is Tuesday's employment and unemployment data for the second quarter, which will be watched closely for confirmation that the labour market can withstand further RBNZ tightening.

currencies.headline: Aussie stays capped near the week's lows as soft China data continues to weigh.
currencies.commentary:
The Australian dollar has remained on the back foot through the session, holding near the lower end of its range for the week after this morning's disappointing Chinese PMI data confirmed a slide back into contraction for the manufacturing sector. The broader risk-on tone in equity markets this afternoon has offered only limited support, underscoring that China-specific weakness, rather than general risk appetite, has been the dominant force on the Aussie this week.

That dynamic reflects the tight link between Australian growth prospects and Chinese industrial demand: with new orders in China's factory survey at their weakest since 2023, the read-through for Australian commodity exports, iron ore and coal in particular, has weighed on sentiment even as a still relatively hawkish Reserve Bank of Australia offers some underlying support. Confirmation, or a contradiction, of today's weak official PMI is likely to come from China's Caixin manufacturing survey on Monday, which skews more toward smaller, export-oriented firms and could move the Aussie meaningfully either way.
currencies.watchToday: Nothing further is scheduled for the Australian dollar today. The next scheduled catalyst is Monday's China Caixin manufacturing PMI, an important cross-reference for this morning's official Chinese data given how closely AUD tracks Chinese industrial sentiment.

currencies.headline: Yuan gains capped as the PBOC sets one of its weakest fixings in months.
currencies.commentary:
The People's Bank of China set its daily reference rate at a notably weaker level than markets expected this morning, the widest weak-side deviation from analyst estimates in around five months, a clear signal that policymakers want to slow the pace of the yuan's advance after the currency touched a fresh multi-year high earlier this week. The move has taken some of the wind out of the yuan's rally through the session, even as broader risk appetite elsewhere improved.

The message is one of managed strength rather than a reversal: officials appear comfortable with a firmer yuan as part of their broader push to project confidence and support capital markets, but are also wary of letting gains run too far, too fast, particularly with today's official PMI data confirming that the underlying manufacturing sector remains under pressure. That combination, a currency trading more on policy signalling than on fundamentals, is likely to keep the yuan somewhat range bound into next week unless the PBoC's fixing bias shifts again.
currencies.watchToday: Nothing further is scheduled for the yuan today. China's Caixin manufacturing PMI, a private sector survey followed closely alongside the official data, is due Monday and will be the next test of whether this week's factory weakness is broad based.

currencies.headline: Rand stays soft after Kganyago's AGM address offers little fresh policy steer.
currencies.commentary:
Governor Lesetja Kganyago's address to the South African Reserve Bank's Annual General Meeting this morning was largely institutional in tone, reflecting on the Bank's history and setting out priorities around the new lower inflation target, financial stability and payments modernisation, rather than offering fresh guidance on the near-term path for interest rates. With no direct steer on the next move, the rand has stayed on the back foot through the session, still digesting last week's surprise decision to hold rates at 7.0% despite inflation running at a two-year high.

That leaves the rand's underlying story unchanged from this morning: a central bank that has so far declined to hike despite hot inflation is effectively allowing the real return on holding the currency to erode, which continues to weigh on demand for it. Kganyago has previously flagged that renewed Middle East tensions and the associated rise in oil and fertiliser costs could yet force the SARB's hand if higher fuel prices feed through to food and core inflation, keeping September's meeting firmly in focus as the next opportunity for a policy shift.
currencies.watchToday: No further South African data or speakers are scheduled today. The next notable release is Monday's Absa/BER manufacturing PMI for July, a lower-tier gauge, with the rand likely to keep taking its broader direction from oil prices and general dollar sentiment into the weekend.

currencies.headline: Sterling holds cautiously steady with all eyes on today's knife edge Bank of England decision.
currencies.commentary:
Sterling has traded in a tight, directionless range overnight as investors square positions ahead of the Bank of England's rate announcement at midday. There is little fresh UK specific news driving the currency this morning; the quiet tone reflects genuine uncertainty about today's outcome rather than complacency. Markets are also still digesting yesterday's Federal Reserve decision, which saw the Fed hold rates under new chair Kevin Warsh without offering much forward guidance, leaving the dollar side of the ledger somewhat unsettled too.

The BoE decision itself is genuinely live. Money markets currently price a clear majority for a hold, but a meaningful minority still see a surprise hike, a legacy of June's split seven to two vote and hawkish commentary from chief economist Huw Pill. A hold with dovish dissent would likely weigh on sterling, while any sign the majority is shifting toward tightening could see it jump. Layered on top is a political dimension: new Prime Minister Andy Burnham, installed after Keir Starmer's June resignation, has signalled a warmer approach to the EU, a theme investors are still working out how to price into the currency over the medium term.
currencies.watchToday: The Bank of England's rate decision lands at 12:00, alongside the Monetary Policy Report, with the Governor's press conference following at 13:00; this is the single biggest event for sterling this week and likely to set the tone into August. Markets are watching the vote split as closely as the decision itself given June's divided committee.

currencies.headline: Euro treads water into a data heavy morning, with Eurozone growth figures the main event.
currencies.commentary:
The euro has been range bound overnight, holding broadly steady after a choppy week that saw it slip toward its softest levels since June before stabilising. The moves have had little to do with the currency bloc itself and much to do with a firmer dollar backdrop ahead of yesterday's Fed decision and today's US growth and inflation data. German retail sales and flash GDP land first thing this morning, followed by the closely watched Eurozone flash GDP print, all released before London's lunch.

The growth data matters because the Eurozone contracted in the first quarter, and today's flash estimate is expected to show only a modest return to growth. A weaker than expected number would revive concerns about the currency bloc's underlying momentum just as markets debate how much further the European Central Bank can diverge from a still cautious Federal Reserve. German flash inflation follows in early afternoon and tends to set the tone for the bloc wide reading due the next day, so a surprise there could easily carry over into tomorrow's session.
currencies.watchToday: German retail sales and flash GDP are due at 07:00, followed by the Eurozone's own flash GDP at 10:00, a speech from ECB chief economist Philip Lane, and German flash CPI at 13:00; it is one of the busiest data mornings of the month for the euro. The bloc wide flash inflation reading follows tomorrow, so today's German number is worth watching as an early signal.

currencies.headline: Dollar steadies after a divided Fed holds rates, with growth and inflation data due later today.
currencies.commentary:
The dollar has traded with a slightly firmer tone overnight, holding onto yesterday's gains as markets continue to digest the Federal Reserve's decision to leave rates unchanged. The meeting was notable less for the outcome, which was widely expected, than for the tone: new Fed chair Kevin Warsh confirmed the committee remains divided and declined to offer much guidance on the path ahead, saying policymakers need to watch how markets and the economy react without pre-committing to a direction. Treasury yields have crept higher since the meeting, a dynamic that has generally supported the currency.

Attention now turns to today's data, where the advance estimate of second quarter GDP and the Fed's preferred core inflation gauge both land at the same time this afternoon. Growth is expected to have picked up from the first quarter's soft pace, while core inflation is forecast to ease slightly from May's reading. Given how tight lipped the new Fed chair was on forward guidance, these numbers carry extra weight for shaping rate expectations into the autumn, and any surprise, particularly on inflation, could move the dollar broadly against all of today's other major currencies.
currencies.watchToday: US second quarter GDP and core PCE inflation both land at 13:30, alongside weekly jobless claims; together they are the most important US release of the week and follow directly on from yesterday's Fed decision. With the new Fed chair offering little forward guidance, today's data will do much of the work of setting near term rate expectations.

currencies.headline: Yen stays soft as traders look ahead to Friday's Bank of Japan decision.
currencies.commentary:
The yen has remained on the back foot overnight, extending a period of broad weakness that has persisted through much of the summer. This morning's national inflation figures for June were the immediate focus, released just ahead of Friday's Bank of Japan meeting, and provided the latest input into how much room the central bank has to keep normalising policy. The currency has struggled to find sustained support even as Japanese inflation measures edge closer to the Bank's target, a sign that yield differentials with the rest of the world are still the dominant force.

The Bank of Japan is widely expected to hold its policy rate steady on Friday after June's quarter point increase, but the broader direction of travel matters more than this single meeting. Underlying inflation is now approaching the Bank's two percent goal, and policymakers have flagged that a persistently weak yen itself risks pushing price growth higher by raising import costs, a feedback loop that could eventually force the Bank's hand. Most analysts still pencil in another hike before year end, which is why every inflation print and BoJ signal is being read closely for timing clues.
currencies.watchToday: Japan's national CPI for June was released early this morning ahead of Friday's Bank of Japan decision, the next major event for the yen; a hold is widely expected but the accompanying guidance will be watched closely for hints on the timing of the next hike. The Governor's press conference follows the decision on Friday.

currencies.headline: Franc stays on the defensive as the SNB's zero rate stance widens the gap with other central banks.
currencies.commentary:
The Swiss franc has drifted lower again overnight, continuing a stretch of underperformance driven less by anything happening in Switzerland and more by what is happening elsewhere. With the Swiss National Bank committed to holding its policy rate at zero and yesterday's Federal Reserve decision doing little to dent expectations for still relatively high US rates, the interest rate gap between Switzerland and its major trading partners has kept widening, and that gap is the single biggest force behind the franc's recent softness.

Swiss inflation slowed to just half a percent in June, comfortably within the SNB's target range and leaving policymakers little reason to shift from their current stance; officials have indicated rates are likely to stay at zero into 2027. The central bank has also made clear it stands ready to smooth disorderly currency swings but has no interest in defending any particular level, which matters because it means the franc's traditional safe haven bid is unlikely to be actively reinforced by policy in the near term, leaving it more exposed to shifts in global risk sentiment and rate differentials than usual.
currencies.watchToday: Nothing is scheduled for the franc today; the next notable release is Friday's KOF Economic Barometer, followed by Swiss CPI on Monday. Until then, the franc is likely to keep taking its cues from the broader dollar and rate differential story rather than domestic news.

currencies.headline: Loonie under pressure as oil retreats on easing Middle East tensions.
currencies.commentary:
The Canadian dollar has softened overnight, weighed down by a sharp pullback in crude oil prices after signs that the ceasefire between the United States and Iran is holding. Brent and WTI have both fallen back substantially from the highs reached during the worst of the recent escalation, and since oil remains one of Canada's most important exports, the currency has moved in step with the retreat. There has been little Canada specific news to offset the move, leaving the loonie largely a function of the global energy market this morning.

The Bank of Canada held its policy rate steady at its last meeting and adopted a more neutral tone, removing the two way guidance it had used previously, while also nudging up its inflation forecast for the year. Domestic inflation actually eased in the latest reading, with core measures at their lowest in more than five years, reinforcing the central bank's view that the earlier spike in energy costs has not spread broadly through the economy. That combination, a patient central bank and now softer oil, leaves the currency more sensitive than usual to swings in crude prices over the coming days.
currencies.watchToday: No major Canadian data is due today; Friday brings GDP by industry figures for May with a June advance estimate, the next real test for the currency. Until then, oil prices and the durability of the Middle East ceasefire remain the dominant drivers.

currencies.headline: Kiwi extends its recovery as hot inflation cements expectations for more RBNZ tightening.
currencies.commentary:
The New Zealand dollar has continued to firm this morning, building on a recovery that began after last month's stronger than expected inflation data and the Reserve Bank of New Zealand's first rate increase in three years. Business confidence has also improved sharply, with a widely watched survey jumping to its highest level since February, helped in part by the recent easing in global oil prices as Middle East tensions have cooled. The combination of hawkish central bank repricing and improving sentiment has given the kiwi one of the stronger runs among the majors over the past few weeks.

Second quarter inflation came in well above both market expectations and the Reserve Bank's own forecast, a clear signal that price pressures are proving stickier than policymakers had hoped. Markets now widely expect another quarter point increase in September, with rates seen climbing further into next year. For a small, commodity sensitive currency like the kiwi, that kind of clear and hawkish policy signal matters more than usual, since it is often the marginal driver that separates New Zealand dollar performance from its Australian counterpart when both currencies are otherwise buffeted by the same global forces.
currencies.watchToday: No major New Zealand data is scheduled this week; the currency is likely to keep trading on the momentum from last month's inflation surprise and shifting expectations for September's Reserve Bank meeting. Broader risk sentiment and moves in commodity prices remain the other key swing factors in the meantime.

currencies.headline: Aussie steady as traders weigh a resilient RBA against a softer China growth backdrop.
currencies.commentary:
The Australian dollar has traded in a narrow range overnight, caught between two offsetting forces. On one side, the Reserve Bank of Australia's cautious but still hawkish tone, having delivered three rate increases earlier this year before pausing to assess their impact, continues to offer some underlying support. On the other, the latest Chinese growth figures showed the world's second largest economy slowing from the first quarter's pace, and since China is Australia's largest trading partner by a wide margin, any wobble there tends to filter through to the currency fairly directly.

Markets currently price only a modest chance of a further RBA hike next month, rising toward year end, so the central bank's cautious wait and see stance is likely to keep the currency more reactive to Chinese data surprises than to domestic developments in the near term. That dynamic is a useful reminder that the Australian dollar behaves as much like a China proxy as a pure interest rate play, which is why Friday's Chinese manufacturing PMI, alongside any signs of fresh stimulus from Beijing, is likely to matter more for the Aussie than anything on the local calendar this week.
currencies.watchToday: No Australian data is due today; China's NBS manufacturing PMI on Friday is the more relevant release for the Aussie given the close trade relationship. Markets continue to price a modest chance of another RBA hike by year end, keeping the currency sensitive to any shift in that outlook.

currencies.headline: Offshore yuan firm as the PBoC keeps steering the currency stronger.
currencies.commentary:
The offshore yuan has held a firm tone overnight, continuing a gradual strengthening trend that has been underway for several weeks. The People's Bank of China has repeatedly set its daily reference rate stronger than expected, a clear signal that policymakers are comfortable with, and to some degree encouraging, a firmer currency even as growth momentum at home remains mixed. Alongside the fixing, authorities have also pushed ahead with measures to deepen offshore yuan liquidity and expand the range of yuan denominated assets available to international investors, part of a broader push to internationalise the currency.

The strategy reflects a balancing act: a stronger yuan helps offset imported inflation and supports confidence in Chinese assets, but it comes at a time when underlying growth is still soft, with subdued consumer demand keeping pressure on policymakers to consider additional support measures. For now, the currency signal from Beijing has been taking precedence over the growth concerns, which is worth watching given how closely the yuan's direction tends to influence sentiment toward other Asia Pacific and commodity linked currencies, including the Australian and New Zealand dollars.
currencies.watchToday: No major Chinese data is due today; the NBS manufacturing PMI on Friday and the Caixin manufacturing PMI on Monday are the next key releases, both important gauges of whether the recent slowdown in growth is stabilising. Until then, the PBoC's daily fixing remains the most immediate signal to watch.

currencies.headline: Rand stays under pressure after the SARB's surprise hold and a firmer dollar backdrop.
currencies.commentary:
The South African rand has remained on the back foot overnight, still digesting last week's surprise decision by the South African Reserve Bank to leave its main interest rate unchanged despite widespread expectations for a hike. That decision, alongside a broadly firmer dollar following yesterday's Federal Reserve meeting, has kept the currency near its softest levels in several months. There has been little fresh domestic news overnight, leaving global dollar dynamics as the main driver of this morning's move.

The SARB's hold came despite inflation accelerating to its highest in two years in June, with core price growth also picking up, both comfortably above the top of the central bank's target range; the decision passed on a split vote, underlining genuine disagreement within the committee about the right path forward. That combination, rising inflation but a central bank reluctant to tighten further, leaves the rand more exposed than most emerging market peers to swings in global risk appetite and US rate expectations, since it offers less of an interest rate cushion to offset any bout of dollar strength.
currencies.watchToday: No major South African data is due today or later this week; the currency is likely to keep trading on broader dollar strength and emerging market risk sentiment rather than domestic catalysts. The next SARB meeting remains some way off, so attention stays on how inflation trends develop into that decision.

currencies.headline: Sterling steadies after a more hawkish than expected Bank of England vote, with Bailey's press conference now the focus.
currencies.commentary:
The Bank of England held Bank Rate at 3.75% as widely expected, but the vote split proved more hawkish than markets had priced, with three of the nine Monetary Policy Committee members voting to raise rates rather than the two or so many analysts had pencilled in. Sterling had a brief, choppy reaction: an initial firming as the hawkish tilt registered, followed by a partial pullback as attention shifted to the accompanying policy report and to broader dollar moves following Wednesday's Federal Reserve decision. Against the euro, sterling has continued to give ground through the session, extending a softening trend that began earlier in the week.

The bigger test for sterling this afternoon is Governor Andrew Bailey's press conference, now under way, where his tone on the vote split and on the balance between still-elevated inflation and a fragile growth and labour market picture will do most of the work in shaping where the pound settles into the weekend. With the Federal Reserve's own guidance this week notably vague, currency markets are leaning more heavily than usual on central bank communication for direction, which raises the stakes for what Bailey says in the coming hour.
currencies.watchToday: Governor Bailey's press conference is under way this hour and remains the key event for sterling today, with his comments on the vote split and inflation outlook likely to matter more than the decision itself. No other major UK data are due before Monday's final manufacturing PMI.

currencies.headline: Euro firms as Eurozone growth surprises strongly to the upside, with German inflation data due imminently.
currencies.commentary:
The euro has firmed through the European session after flash data showed the Eurozone economy grew 0.4% quarter on quarter in the second quarter, well above the roughly 0.2% pace economists had expected and a clear improvement on a flat first quarter. Annual growth accelerated to 1.0% from 0.5%, and the pickup was broad based, with Spain and Portugal continuing to outperform and France returning to growth after a first quarter contraction. The data followed an encouraging German GDP print earlier in the morning and has reinforced the sense that the currency bloc is weathering trade and energy pressures better than feared.

The other side of today's story is inflation. German flash consumer prices for July are due within the hour, with economists looking for a pickup toward 2.8% year on year from 2.4% in June as a temporary fuel duty cut drops out of the comparison. Stronger growth alongside firmer inflation would reinforce bets that the ECB has room to keep raising rates even as the Federal Reserve's own path looks murkier after an unusually non-committal press conference from its new chair on Wednesday, a contrast that has been broadly supportive for the euro today.
currencies.watchToday: German flash inflation for July lands this hour and could add to the euro's momentum if it confirms the expected pickup toward 2.8%. The bigger release is tomorrow's Eurozone-wide flash inflation print at 10:00, alongside the Eurozone unemployment rate, both important inputs into the ECB's next move.

currencies.headline: Dollar steadies after its sharpest post-Fed drop in weeks, with growth and inflation data due within the half hour.
currencies.commentary:
The dollar has clawed back some of Wednesday's losses this morning after tumbling to its weakest level since 20 July following the Federal Reserve's decision to hold rates at 3.50% to 3.75%. New chair Kevin Warsh again declined to offer clear forward guidance, arguing instead that the recent rise in market interest rates has already tightened financial conditions on the Fed's behalf. Traders read that as dovish and pared back the probability of a September rate rise, while three regional Fed presidents voted for an immediate hike, underlining how divided the committee remains. Longer-dated Treasury yields jumped in response, with the 30-year yield reaching its highest level since 2007, a split reaction that speaks to markets questioning the Fed's credibility rather than its near-term rate path alone.

Renewed fighting in the Middle East has added a further complication, pushing oil prices higher again and threatening to keep inflation elevated regardless of what the Fed does next. That combination has left the dollar searching for direction into this afternoon's data. The advance estimate of second quarter GDP and the Fed's preferred core inflation gauge for June both land within the next half hour, followed by weekly jobless claims, and together they will shape how much credibility markets attach to a September move.
currencies.watchToday: US second quarter GDP and core PCE inflation for June both land at 13:30, with weekly jobless claims at the same time; this is the most important data of the week for rate expectations given how little guidance the Fed offered on Wednesday. A quieter Chicago PMI follows tomorrow afternoon.

currencies.headline: Yen holds a narrow range as traders brace for tomorrow's Bank of Japan decision.
currencies.commentary:
The yen has traded in a tight band through the session, caught between two competing forces. On one side, renewed Middle East tensions and a wobblier tone in global equity markets have offered some safe-haven support; on the other, Japan's interest rate remains far below its major-economy peers, and fresh reports that Tokyo is considering a temporary cut to the sales tax on food have raised fresh questions about the government's fiscal discipline, a negative for the currency. The net effect has been a currency largely marking time near its softest levels in decades, with little conviction in either direction ahead of tomorrow's policy decision.
